decks.title: A World of Many Cultures

slides.title: In this lesson you will

slides.title: What do we mean by culture?

cards.heading: What we can see
cards.text: Food, dress, music, festivals, language: the visible tip of the **iceberg**.
cards.example: Santos Populares, sardines and manjericos

cards.heading: What lies beneath
cards.text: Values, attitudes to time, family, authority and personal space.
cards.example: Is being ten minutes late rude or normal?

cards.heading: It keeps changing
cards.text: Cultures borrow, mix and evolve. No culture is frozen or **pure**.
cards.example: Pastéis de nata are now sold in Tokyo and London.

slides.instruction: Complete the sentences with words from the box.

left.heading: Stereotype
points: A fixed idea applied to **every** member of a group
Ignores evidence and individual differences
Often hidden in jokes: "All Portuguese are late."
Closes the conversation

right.heading: Generalisation
points: A **tendency** based on evidence, open to exceptions
Uses hedging: **tend to**, **on the whole**, **many**
"Lunch in Portugal tends to be later than in the UK."
Opens the conversation

slides.title: Hedging: sound fair, not naive
slides.text: In essays and debates, **soften** claims about groups of people. Examiners reward this kind of precision.
examples: Many British people **tend to** apologise when they bump into you.
Family meals **are generally seen as** important in southern Europe.
**It could be argued that** social media spreads stereotypes faster.
**In my experience**, people in Porto are very direct.

slides.title: Make it a fair generalisation
slides.instruction: Rewrite each stereotype as a hedged generalisation. Use the word in brackets.

items.q: Germans are always on time. (tend)
Teenagers are addicted to their phones. (many)
items.a: Many teenagers spend a lot of time on their phones.

items.q: Americans don't know anything about Europe. (some)
items.a: Some Americans know relatively little about Europe.

items.q: Older people hate change. (often)
items.a: Older people are often more cautious about change.

slides.title: Third culture kids
text: Inês was born in Luanda, grew up in Maputo and moved to Lisbon at fourteen. When people ask where she is from, she hesitates. Sociologists call people like her **third culture kids**: children who spend their formative years outside their parents' culture.

Research suggests they adapt quickly, read social cues well and often speak several languages. The cost is a sense of **rootlessness**. Many feel at home everywhere and nowhere, and they tend to bond with other people who have moved around.
"I used to envy friends who had lived in one street all their lives," Inês says. "Now I think home is people, not a place."

slides.title: Reading comprehension
slides.instruction: Decide if the statements are true (T) or false (F). Correct the false ones.

items.q: Inês has lived in three different countries.
Third culture kids grow up inside their parents' culture.
items.fix: They spend their formative years outside their parents' culture.

items.q: The text says they usually speak only one language.
items.fix: They often speak several languages.

items.q: Many feel they do not fully belong anywhere.
Inês now links the idea of home to a particular city.
items.fix: She now thinks home is people, not a place.

left.heading: Appropriation
points: Taking sacred or meaningful symbols as a costume
Profiting while the source community is ignored
No credit, no context, no understanding

right.heading: Appreciation
points: Learning the history behind a tradition
Credits and pays the people who created it
Joins in when invited, on their terms

slides.title: Remember
points: Culture includes visible habits and **invisible values**.
A **stereotype** fixes a label; a **generalisation** allows exceptions.
Hedge claims: **tend to**, **generally**, **many**, **it could be argued**.

slides.title: The five-euro T-shirt
text: A T-shirt for five euros feels like a bargain until you follow it back along the supply chain. Cotton needs huge amounts of water to grow. The fabric is often dyed in factories that release chemicals into rivers, and the people who sew it may earn very little.

Fast-fashion brands release new collections every few weeks, so clothes are treated as disposable. Most of what we throw away is never recycled into new clothes: it is burnt, sent to landfill or shipped abroad.
The alternatives are not glamorous: buy less, buy second-hand, repair what you have. The cheapest T-shirt, environmentally speaking, is the one already in your wardrobe.

slides.title: Check your understanding
slides.instruction: Answer the questions in your own words.

items.q: Why is the T-shirt only apparently a bargain?
items.a: Because its real costs (water, pollution, low wages) are paid by others along the supply chain.

items.q: What makes fast fashion feel disposable?
items.a: Brands release new collections every few weeks, so clothes seem out of date quickly.

items.q: What happens to most discarded clothes?
items.a: They are burnt, sent to landfill or shipped abroad, not recycled into new clothes.

items.q: What does the last sentence mean?
items.a: Using clothes you already own has the lowest environmental impact.

slides.title: Useful structures for argument
rows: **Admittedly**, cheap clothes help families on a budget.
**Even so**, the real cost is paid by someone else.
**If** brands **were** taxed on waste, they **would** change.
slides.note: Use a concession before your counter-argument: it makes your position stronger, not weaker.

slides.title: Editing life
text: In 2020 Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing CRISPR, a tool that can cut and change DNA with remarkable precision. Scientists often compare it to the find-and-replace function in a word processor.
Its supporters see enormous potential: treating inherited diseases, creating crops that resist drought, perhaps even stopping mosquitoes from spreading malaria.

Critics are uneasy. Changes made to embryos would be passed on to future generations, and nobody can predict every consequence. There is also the fear of "designer babies", where wealthy parents choose traits for their children. The science is moving faster than the law.

slides.instruction: Choose the option that best completes each sentence according to the text.

items.q: Robots probably won't replace teachers. (unlikely)

slides.title: Debate

**likely to** (probable), **bound to** (almost certain), **set to** (planned).
Future perfect: **By 2040** we **will have** + past participle.
Weigh benefits and risks before you take a position.

slides.title: Watch out: false friends
slides.text: Some work words look Portuguese but mean something else. Check before you use them in an interview.
examples: **Résumé / CV** is the document, **not** a summary of a book.
**Actually** means "na verdade", not "atualmente" (**currently**).

A **lecture** is a talk at university; "leitura" is **reading**.

Social security and sick pay
Fixed hours and a commute

right.heading: Gig and platform work

slides.title: The four-day week
text: Several countries, Portugal included, have tested a four-day working week with no cut in pay. In most trials, companies and employees agreed in advance to keep the same output in fewer hours.
Many participants reported less stress and better sleep, and some companies found it easier to hire. Meetings got shorter and people protected their focus time.

Sceptics point out that the model fits offices better than hospitals, shops or schools, where someone has to be there. Others fear that squeezing five days of work into four simply makes each day more intense. The debate is less about one day off than about what we really pay people for: their time or their results.

slides.title: Reading comprehension
slides.instruction: Decide if the statements are true (T) or false (F). Correct the false ones.

items.q: In the trials, workers earned less for the shorter week.
items.fix: There was no cut in pay.

items.q: Some companies found recruitment easier.

items.fix: It fits offices better than hospitals, shops or schools.

items.q: Some people fear the remaining days become more intense.
The writer says the real issue is paying for time or results.

slides.title: The Windrush generation
text: In June 1948 the ship Empire Windrush arrived in Britain carrying hundreds of passengers from the Caribbean. They had been invited to help rebuild the country after the Second World War, and many went on to work in hospitals, on buses and in factories.
They were British subjects with the right to live in the UK, but many faced open racism when looking for housing or work.

Decades later, in 2018, a scandal revealed that some of them and their children had been wrongly classified as illegal immigrants. Several lost their jobs or were detained, and some were deported, despite having lived in Britain almost all their lives. The government apologised, and a compensation scheme was set up.

items.q: Many of them worked in public services.
The 2018 scandal involved people born recently abroad.
items.fix: It involved people who had lived in Britain almost all their lives.

items.q: The government later offered compensation.

slides.title: Votes at 16?
text: In Portugal you can vote from the age of 18. Some countries have gone further: Austria lowered its voting age to 16 for national elections in 2007, and in Scotland 16-year-olds can vote in Scottish Parliament elections.

Supporters argue that teenagers already pay taxes when they work and will live longest with the consequences of today's decisions on climate, housing and pensions. Voting early, they say, creates a lifelong habit.

Opponents reply that most 16-year-olds are not yet financially independent and may simply copy their parents' views. Others note that young adults already have the lowest turnout, so the real problem is engagement, not age.

decks.title: Global Sustainability

cards.example: Goal 13: Climate Action

cards.heading: The Paris Agreement
cards.text: Also 2015: keep warming **well below 2°C** and try to limit it to 1.5°C.
cards.example: Countries set their own targets.

cards.example: Economy, society, environment

slides.title: Which goal is it?
slides.instruction: Match each situation with the Sustainable Development Goal it relates to.

items.q: Girls in some countries leave school early.

slides.title: Small islands, big questions
text: Tuvalu, a Pacific nation of nine small islands, is among the countries most threatened by rising seas. Much of its land is only a few metres above sea level, and its people have contributed almost nothing to global emissions.

This is the heart of **climate justice**: the countries that have burnt the most fossil fuels for longest are generally richer and better able to protect themselves, while poorer nations suffer first and worst.
At international summits, vulnerable countries ask for more than sympathy. They want funding to adapt, compensation for loss and damage, and faster cuts in emissions from the biggest polluters.

slides.title: Reading comprehension
slides.instruction: Answer the questions according to the text.

items.q: Why is Tuvalu especially at risk?
items.a: Much of its land is only a few metres above sea level, so rising seas threaten it.

items.q: What is unfair about Tuvalu's situation?
items.a: It has contributed almost nothing to emissions but suffers some of the worst effects.

items.q: Explain climate justice in your own words.
items.a: Those who caused most of the problem should do most to fix it and help those affected.

items.q: Name two things vulnerable countries ask for.
items.a: Any two: funding to adapt, compensation for loss and damage, faster emission cuts.

slides.title: Making conditions and proposals
rows: I'll fly less **provided that** trains get cheaper.
People recycle **as long as** it's easy.
Act now; **otherwise** it will cost more.
Towns build walls **in case** of floods.
slides.note: After unless, provided and as long as, use a present tense for the future: unless we act, NOT unless we will act.

slides.title: Unless = if... not
slides.text: Do not add another negative after **unless**. The negative meaning is already inside the word.
examples: **Unless** we act now, it will be too late.
Not: Unless we don't act now...
= **If** we **don't** act now, it will be too late.

slides.title: Conditions
slides.instruction: Rewrite the sentences using the word in brackets. Keep the meaning.

items.q: If we don't cut emissions, sea levels will keep rising. (unless)
items.a: Unless we cut emissions, sea levels will keep rising.

items.q: I'll take the train only if it isn't too expensive. (provided)
items.a: I'll take the train provided (that) it isn't too expensive.

items.q: Take a water bottle. There may be no fountains. (in case)
items.a: Take a water bottle in case there are no fountains.

items.q: We must invest in solar. If not, bills will rise. (otherwise)
items.a: We must invest in solar; otherwise, bills will rise.

slides.title: Choose the linker
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

items.q: Crops will fail ___ it rains soon.
You can borrow my bike ___ you bring it back.
Keep some candles ___ there's a power cut.
Unless the city ___ more trees, it will overheat.

slides.title: Discussion
questions: Should rich countries pay for climate damage in poorer ones?
Which SDG do you think Portugal is furthest from reaching?
Is individual action meaningful, or only government action?
Would you give up flying for a year? Under what conditions?
Should countries offer residency to climate refugees?

slides.title: Remember
points: **17 SDGs**, adopted in 2015, with a 2030 deadline.
**Climate justice**: those who polluted most should do most.
**unless** = if not; **provided / as long as** = only if; **in case** = precaution.
No future **will** after unless, provided or as long as.

discuss **brain drain** and **digital nomads** in Portugal
notice how **work cultures** differ between countries
adapt your language to sound **diplomatic** at work

cards.heading: Erasmus+
cards.text: EU programme for studying, training or volunteering in another country.
cards.example: A semester in Ghent or Kraków

cards.heading: Free movement
cards.text: EU citizens can live and work in any EU country without a work permit.
cards.example: A nurse from Coimbra working in Paris

cards.heading: Visas
cards.text: Outside the EU you usually need a visa or permit. Since Brexit, this includes the UK.
cards.example: Applying for a skilled worker visa

slides.title: Vocabulary check
slides.instruction: Complete the sentences with words from the vocabulary slide.

items.q: She got a ___ from a company in Amsterdam.

slides.title: Leaving and arriving
text: Every year thousands of young Portuguese graduates, many of them nurses, engineers and doctors, move abroad in search of higher salaries and better career prospects. Their education was largely paid for by Portuguese taxpayers, and the benefits go elsewhere.

At the same time, Lisbon and Porto have become magnets for **digital nomads**: remote workers who earn foreign salaries while living in Portugal. They bring spending and new businesses, but in central neighbourhoods they have also added pressure on rents that local workers struggle to pay.
Two movements, one question: how can a country keep its own talent while staying open to the world?

slides.title: Reading comprehension
slides.instruction: Decide if the statements are true (T) or false (F). Correct the false ones.

items.q: Young graduates mainly leave to see the world.

left.heading: More direct
points: Say exactly what you mean
Criticism given openly in meetings
"This report has three mistakes."
Often associated with Dutch or German workplaces

right.heading: More indirect
points: Meaning depends on context and tone
Criticism softened or given in private
"Perhaps we could look at this again?"
Often associated with British or Japanese workplaces

slides.title: What the British say, and mean
slides.text: British English at work is often **understated**. Learn to read between the lines, and to soften your own requests.
examples: "**That's an interesting idea.**" Possible meaning: I don't like it.
"**I'd suggest** we think about it." Meaning: Please change it.
"**With the greatest respect**..." Meaning: I strongly disagree.
"**Not bad at all.**" Meaning: This is very good.

"Quite good" in a British performance review

slides.title: Remember
points: EU citizens enjoy **free movement**; elsewhere you need a **work permit**.
**Brain drain** and **digital nomads** are two sides of mobility.
Work cultures vary from **direct** to **indirect**.
Soften requests: **Could you**...? **I'm not sure**... **We might**...

decks.title: Impersonal Passive
decks.subtitle: It is said that... but who said it?

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: report opinions and rumours with **It is said that**...
use the personal structure **He is said to**...
choose the right infinitive: **to do, to be doing, to have done**
recognise this structure in **news** and **academic** writing

cards.heading: News reports
cards.text: The source is unknown, unimportant or cannot be named.
cards.example: The minister **is reported to** be resigning.

cards.heading: Distance
cards.text: The writer does not take responsibility for the claim.
cards.example: **It is alleged that** he stole the files.

cards.heading: Formal writing
cards.text: Essays and reports avoid "people say" and "they think".
cards.example: **It is widely believed that**...

slides.title: Two structures, same meaning
rows: **It is said that** he is rich.
**It is believed that** she lives abroad.
**It is expected that** prices will rise.
**It was thought that** it was haunted.
slides.note: Common verbs: say, think, believe, know, report, expect, consider, claim, allege, estimate, understand.

slides.title: Structure 1: It is said that...
slides.instruction: Rewrite the sentences starting with It. Keep the tense of the reporting verb.

items.q: People say that the castle is 800 years old.
items.a: It is said that the castle is 800 years old.

items.q: Experts believe the drought will continue.
items.a: It is believed that the drought will continue.

items.q: They reported that two climbers were missing.
items.a: It was reported that two climbers were missing.

items.q: Everyone knows that sugar is bad for teeth.
items.a: It is known that sugar is bad for teeth.

slides.title: Structure 2: which infinitive?
rows: She **is said to speak** six languages.
They **are thought to be hiding** in Spain.
He **is believed to have left** last night.
She **is said to have been working** there for years.
The bridge **is expected to open** in May.
slides.note: The reporting verb shows WHEN people say it; the infinitive shows WHEN the action happens.

slides.title: Watch out!
slides.text: If the reported action happened **before**, you need **to have + past participle**. A simple infinitive changes the meaning.
examples: People think he **stole** the money.
He is thought **to have stolen** the money. (correct)
He is thought to steal money. (= a habit, now)

slides.title: Choose the right infinitive
slides.instruction: Complete with the correct form of the verb in brackets.

items.q: The thief is believed ___ the country yesterday. (leave)
Ronaldo is known ___ very hard every day. (train)
The two leaders are said ___ a deal right now. (negotiate)
Over 300 people are reported ___ in the floods. (die)
The new metro line is expected ___ in 2027. (open)
He is thought ___ for the CIA for years. (work)

slides.title: Structure 2: He is said to...
slides.instruction: Rewrite the sentences starting with the subject given in brackets.

items.q: It is said that the band is splitting up. (The band)
items.a: The band is said to be splitting up.

items.q: It is believed that the painting was stolen in 1990. (The painting)
items.a: The painting is believed to have been stolen in 1990.

items.q: People think the mayor knew about the fraud. (The mayor)
items.a: The mayor is thought to have known about the fraud.

items.q: Experts estimate that the trip costs 5,000 euros. (The trip)
items.a: The trip is estimated to cost 5,000 euros.

items.q: It was reported that the suspect was armed. (The suspect)
items.a: The suspect was reported to be armed.

items.en: People say there is a secret tunnel. → **There is said to be** a secret tunnel.
They think there are wolves nearby. → **There are thought to be** wolves nearby.
Reports say there were 50 cars involved. → **There are reported to have been** 50 cars involved.
**It is estimated that** there are 8,000 species. → **There are estimated to be** 8,000 species.

slides.title: Find the correct sentence
slides.instruction: Choose the grammatically correct option.

items.q: People say there is gold in the hills.
options: There is said to be gold in the hills.
It is said to be gold in the hills.
Gold says to be in the hills.
items.a: There is said to be gold in the hills.

items.q: They believe the ship sank in 1700.
options: The ship is believed to sink in 1700.
The ship is believed to have sunk in 1700.
The ship believes to have sunk in 1700.
items.a: The ship is believed to have sunk in 1700.

items.q: It is thought that she is living in Porto.
options: She is thought to living in Porto.
She is thought to be living in Porto.
She thought to be living in Porto.
items.a: She is thought to be living in Porto.

slides.title: Remember
points: **It is said / believed / thought that** + full clause.
Subject + **is said / believed to** + infinitive.
Earlier action: **to have + past participle** (to have left).
With there: **There is said to be**...

decks.title: Wishes and Regrets
decks.subtitle: If only I had studied for that test...

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: express wishes about the **present** and regrets about the **past**
complain about other people's habits with **wish + would**
state preferences with **I'd rather**
say that something should happen now with **It's time**

slides.title: Wish and if only
rows: present situation you'd like to change
slides.note: **If only** uses the same tenses but is more emotional: If only I **had listened**!

slides.title: The past is not the past
slides.text: After **wish**, we go **one tense back** to show something is unreal. The past simple talks about **now**.
examples: I wish I **knew** the answer. (I don't know it now.)
I wish I **had known** the answer. (I didn't know it then.)
**Were** is preferred in formal English: I wish he **were** here.

slides.title: Present or past?
slides.instruction: Complete with the correct form of the verb in brackets.

items.q: I wish I ___ (live) closer to the beach. The bus takes ages.
She wishes she ___ (not / eat) that pizza last night.
If only we ___ (be) on holiday right now!
I wish I ___ (can) play the guitar like my cousin.
If only I ___ (buy) the tickets when they were cheap.
He wishes he ___ (know) her number. He'd call her now.

slides.title: Wish + would: be careful
slides.text: Use **wish + would** for other people's behaviour or things you want to change. Do not use it about yourself.
examples: I wish my brother **would** knock before coming in.
I wish it **would** stop raining. (I want a change.)
Not: I wish I would... Use: I wish I **could** / I **were**...

slides.title: Express the wish
slides.instruction: Write a sentence with wish for each situation.

items.q: I don't have enough money for the festival.
items.a: I wish I had enough money for the festival.

items.q: My neighbour plays loud music every night.
items.a: I wish my neighbour wouldn't play loud music every night.

items.q: I didn't go to the concert. Now I regret it.
items.a: I wish I had gone to the concert.

items.q: I can't drive yet.
You always leave your socks on the floor.
items.a: I wish you wouldn't leave your socks on the floor.

slides.title: I'd rather
rows: I'd rather **walk than take** the bus.
slides.note: **Would prefer** takes to: I'd prefer to stay in. I'd prefer you not to tell anyone.

slides.title: Preferences
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

items.q: I'd rather ___ at home tonight.
I'd rather you ___ my phone without asking.
She'd rather ___ than go by car.
I'd rather you ___ me yesterday. It was a surprise.
I'd prefer ___ this alone.

items.en: **It's time we went** home. (subject + past simple, present meaning)
**It's high time** the government **did** something about rents. (criticism)

slides.title: It's time...
slides.instruction: Rewrite the sentences using the words in brackets.

items.q: You should go to bed now. (time)
items.a: It's time you went to bed.

items.q: The council should fix this road. It's late! (high time)
items.a: It's high time the council fixed this road.

items.q: We need to leave now. (time to)
You should really tidy your room. (about time)
items.a: It's about time you tidied your room.

slides.title: Your turn
questions: What do you wish you could change about your school?
Is there anything you wish you had done differently last year?
Complete: "I wish people would..."
Would you rather live in Lisbon or in a small village? Why?
What is it high time Portugal did something about?

slides.title: Remember
points: **wish + past simple** (now), **wish + past perfect** (past regret).
**wish + would** for other people's annoying habits.
I'd rather **stay**; I'd rather **you stayed**; I'd rather you **hadn't**...
It's (high) time **we went**, or It's time **to go**.

decks.title: Inversion
decks.subtitle: Never have I seen a sentence quite like this one

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: invert subject and auxiliary after **negative adverbials**
use **No sooner... than** and **Hardly... when**
use **Not until** and **Only** + time expression
replace if with **Had I**, **Should you** and **Were I**

cards.heading: Question word order
cards.text: After certain words at the start, the **auxiliary** comes before the **subject**, like in a question.
cards.example: **Never have I** felt so cold.

cards.heading: Formal and dramatic
cards.text: Typical of speeches, essays, news and literature. It adds **emphasis**.
cards.example: **Rarely does** a team win twice.

cards.heading: No auxiliary?
cards.text: In the present and past simple, add **do / does / did**.
cards.example: **Little did she** know the truth.

slides.title: Negative and limiting adverbials
rows: **Not only did she** win, **but** she **also** broke the record.
**Under no circumstances should you** open this door.
On no account / At no time
**At no time was** the public at risk.
**Not once did he** say thank you.
slides.note: Only the auxiliary moves: Not only did she win (NOT Not only won she).

slides.title: Emphasise it
slides.instruction: Rewrite the sentences beginning with the words given.

items.q: I have never seen so many people in Rossio. (Never)
items.a: Never have I seen so many people in Rossio.

items.q: We rarely eat out during the week. (Rarely)
items.a: Rarely do we eat out during the week.

items.q: She didn't know that he was lying. (Little)
items.a: Little did she know that he was lying.

items.q: You must not touch this button. (Under no circumstances)
items.a: Under no circumstances must you touch this button.

items.q: He's a great singer and he also plays drums. (Not only)
items.a: Not only is he a great singer, but he also plays drums.

slides.title: Time: one thing after another
rows: **No sooner had** we arrived **than** it started to rain.
**Hardly had** I sat down **when** the phone rang.
**Not until** I left home **did I** value my mum's cooking.
**Only when** the lights went out **did** we panic.
**Only later did** I understand his warning.
slides.note: No sooner goes with **than**; Hardly and Scarcely go with **when**. Do not mix them.

slides.title: Where does the inversion go?
slides.text: With **Not until** and **Only when / after**, the inversion is in the **main clause**, not in the first clause.
examples: Only after the match **ended did** the fans leave.
Not: Only after **did the match end** the fans left.
Not until you apologise **will I** speak to you again.

slides.title: Complete the inversion
slides.instruction: Complete each gap with a word from the box. Words can be used more than once.

items.q: No sooner had the film started ___ the power went off.
Hardly had she left ___ it began to snow.
Not until midnight ___ we finish the project.
Only after a long wait ___ the doctor call us in.
Seldom ___ you find such a quiet beach in August.
Not only ___ she sing, but she also writes her own songs.

slides.title: Conditional inversion (no if)
rows: **If I had known**, I would have helped.
**Had I known**, I would have helped.
**Had he not** warned us... (NOT Hadn't he)
slides.note: Only had, should and were can replace if in this way.

slides.title: Drop the if
slides.instruction: Rewrite the conditional sentences without if.

items.q: If I had studied more, I would have passed.
items.a: Had I studied more, I would have passed.

items.q: If you have any questions, please contact us.
items.a: Should you have any questions, please contact us.

items.q: If I were the mayor, I would build more cycle lanes.
items.a: Were I the mayor, I would build more cycle lanes.

items.q: If they hadn't missed the penalty, they would have won.
items.a: Had they not missed the penalty, they would have won.

slides.title: Correct or incorrect?
slides.instruction: Choose the correct sentence.

items.q: Which is correct?
options: Never I have been so tired.
Never have I been so tired.
items.a: Never have I been so tired.

items.q: Which is correct?
options: Hardly had I arrived than he left.
Hardly had I arrived when he left.
items.a: Hardly had I arrived when he left.

items.q: Which is correct?
Which is correct?
options: Hadn't she called, we'd have gone.
Had she not called, we'd have gone.
items.a: Had she not called, we'd have gone.

slides.title: Put the words in order
slides.instruction: Order the words to make inverted sentences.

items.q: had / sooner / No / home / I / got / than / rang / she
items.a: No sooner had I got home than she rang.

items.q: did / Little / they / the / was / test / know / cancelled
items.a: Little did they know the test was cancelled.

items.q: account / On / you / no / should / your / share / password
items.a: On no account should you share your password.

slides.title: Remember
points: Negative adverbial at the start + **auxiliary + subject**.
No auxiliary? Use **do / does / did**: Little **did** I know.
**No sooner... than**; **Hardly / Scarcely... when**.
**Had I known**, **Should you need**, **Were I you**: if disappears.

decks.title: Gerund or Infinitive?
decks.subtitle: Did you stop to smoke, or stop smoking?

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: see how **remember, forget, stop** and **try** change meaning
use **regret, go on, mean** and **need** correctly
avoid common mistakes Portuguese speakers make
tell a short story using both forms

slides.title: The basic logic
slides.text: Very often the **-ing** form looks **back** at an action that already happened, and **to + infinitive** looks **forward** to an action still to do.
examples: I remember **locking** the door. (I locked it, and I have that memory.)
Remember **to lock** the door. (Don't forget the task.)

slides.title: Remember, forget, regret
rows: I'll never forget **seeing** the sea for the first time.
I regret **saying** that to him. (I'm sorry I did.)
We regret **to inform** you that... (formal bad news)
slides.note: Forget + -ing is mostly used with never: I'll never forget... In other cases, use don't remember.

slides.title: Stop, try, go on
rows: He stopped **to smoke**. (He paused in order to smoke.)
Try **drinking** tea. (an experiment: see if it helps)
I tried **to open** it. (an effort, maybe it failed)
She went on **talking**. (continued the same thing)
She went on **to become** a judge. (next step)

slides.title: Which meaning?
slides.instruction: Choose the correct form for each context.

items.q: Don't forget ___ the bins out tonight.
I remember ___ my first goal. I was eight.
We stopped ___ a coffee on the way to Faro.
Doctors told him to stop ___ so much sugar.
If the Wi-Fi fails, try ___ the router.
I tried ___ the jar, but it was stuck.

slides.title: Mean, need, like
rows: A new job means **moving** to Braga. (involves)
I like **to see** the dentist twice a year. (good idea)
slides.note: Needs washing = needs to be washed. Both are correct in British English.

slides.title: Complete the sentences
slides.instruction: Complete with the correct form of the verb in brackets.

items.q: Sorry, I didn't mean ___ (wake) you up.
Studying medicine means ___ (work) very long hours.
Your hair needs ___ (cut). It's in your eyes!
After school, she went on ___ (study) law in Coimbra.
I regret ___ (not / go) to the Erasmus meeting.
We regret ___ (announce) that the 8.15 train is cancelled.

slides.title: Match the meaning
slides.instruction: Match each sentence with its meaning.

items.q: He stopped to talk to her.
items.a: He paused to have a chat.

items.q: He stopped talking to her.
items.a: They are no longer in contact.

items.q: She went on singing.
She went on to sing opera.
I tried to call him.
items.a: I made an effort to reach him.

items.q: I tried calling him.

slides.title: Watch out!
slides.text: Portuguese uses the infinitive in many places where English needs **-ing**. Translate with care.
examples: Lembro-me de ter visto... = I remember **seeing**...
Parei de fumar. = I stopped **smoking**.
Arrependo-me de ter dito. = I regret **saying** / **having said** it.

slides.title: Rewrite with the same meaning
slides.instruction: Rewrite the sentences using the verb in brackets.

items.q: I locked the car. I can picture it clearly. (remember)
I'm sorry I told you the secret. (regret)
items.a: I regret telling you the secret.

items.q: Don't forget to text me when you arrive. (remember)
items.a: Remember to text me when you arrive.

items.q: The walls should be painted. (need)
It wasn't my intention to break the vase. (mean)
items.a: I didn't mean to break the vase.

slides.title: Your turn
questions: What do you remember doing on your first day of school?
Is there anything you regret not doing last summer?
What should you remember to do before an exam?
Have you ever tried studying with music? Did it help?
What would you like to stop doing, and why?

slides.title: Remember
points: **-ing** looks back; **to + infinitive** looks forward.
stop **doing** (quit) vs stop **to do** (pause in order to).
try **doing** (experiment) vs try **to do** (effort).
need **doing** = needs to be done; mean **doing** = involve.

decks.title: The Causative
decks.subtitle: Did you cut your hair, or did you have it cut?

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: say that someone does a service for you: **have / get something done**
talk about bad experiences: **I had my bag stolen**
use **have someone do** and **get someone to do**
compare **make** and **let** + object + bare infinitive

left.heading: You did it
points: I **cut** my hair. (with my own scissors!)
She **repaired** her bike.
We **painted** the living room.

right.heading: Someone did it for you
points: I **had my hair cut**. (at the hairdresser's)
She **got her bike repaired**.
We **had the living room painted**.

slides.title: Form: have / get + object + past participle
rows: She **got** her nails **done** for the wedding.
I**'m going to get** my phone screen **fixed**.
slides.note: The object goes BEFORE the participle: I had my hair cut, NOT I had cut my hair.

slides.title: Services
slides.instruction: Rewrite the sentences using the causative with have.

items.q: A mechanic is checking our brakes.
items.a: We are having our brakes checked.

items.q: A photographer took Rita's passport photo.
items.a: Rita had her passport photo taken.

items.q: A tailor will shorten my trousers.
items.a: I will have my trousers shortened.

items.q: An electrician has repaired our lights.
items.a: We have had our lights repaired.

items.q: Someone delivers the newspaper to Grandpa every day.
items.a: Grandpa has the newspaper delivered every day.

slides.title: When things go wrong
slides.text: The same structure describes **unpleasant things that happen to you**, done by someone else. No service, no choice.
examples: I **had my phone stolen** on the metro.
He **had his car broken into** last night.
She **got her flight cancelled** twice.

slides.title: Complete the causative
slides.instruction: Complete with the correct form of have and the verb in brackets.

items.q: I can't see well. I need to ___ my eyes ___ (test).
Last week she ___ her wallet ___ (steal) at the market.
We ___ currently ___ our kitchen ___ (redo).
Where did you ___ your hair ___ (dye)?
They've just ___ a new boiler ___ (install).

slides.title: Making people do things
rows: I **got** my dad **to lend** me the car.
My parents **let** me **go** to the festival.
slides.note: In the passive, make takes to: We were made to run 10 km. Let has no passive: use be allowed to.

slides.title: Have, get, make or let?
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

items.q: The teacher made us ___ the essay again.
I finally got my brother ___ me his hoodie.
Mum won't ___ me stay out after midnight.
We were made ___ in the rain for an hour.
The manager had the receptionist ___ a taxi.

slides.title: Put the words in order
slides.instruction: Order the words to make correct sentences.

items.q: had / We / our / house / last / painted / summer
items.a: We had our house painted last summer.

items.q: got / my / I / to / friend / help / me / move
items.a: I got my friend to help me move.

items.q: you / should / that / get / checked / cough
items.a: You should get that cough checked.

items.q: let / didn't / us / The / use / phones / teacher
items.a: The teacher didn't let us use phones.

slides.title: Your turn
questions: What services do you regularly have done? Haircut, nails, bike?
Have you ever had anything stolen? What happened?
What do your parents make you do that you'd rather not?
What would you like your parents to let you do?
How did you last get someone to do you a favour?

slides.title: Remember
points: **have / get + object + past participle**: a service or a misfortune.
**have** someone **do**; **get** someone **to do**.
**make** (force) and **let** (allow) + bare infinitive.
Passive: **be made to** do; **be allowed to** do (not be let).

decks.title: Modal Verbs Review
decks.subtitle: He must have forgotten... or might he have lied?

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: review modals of **obligation, permission** and **advice**
make **deductions** about the present and the past
tell **needn't have done** from **didn't need to do**
criticise and regret with **should have** and **could have**

slides.title: Obligation, prohibition, advice
rows: You **mustn't** use phones in the exam.
You **don't have to** come. It's optional.
You**'d better** leave now or you'll miss it.
slides.note: Mustn't = proibido. Don't have to = não é preciso. They are NOT the same.

slides.title: Rules and advice
slides.instruction: Choose the best option.

items.q: You ___ smoke inside a restaurant. It's illegal.
It's Saturday, so I ___ get up early.
In the UK, drivers ___ drive on the left.
You look exhausted. You ___ go to bed.
We ___ hurry, or we'll miss the last bus.

slides.title: Deduction: how sure are you?
rows: almost sure it is NOT true
It **can't be** Rui. He's in Paris.
slides.note: The negative of must for deduction is can't, not mustn't: He can't be serious!

slides.title: Make deductions
slides.instruction: Rewrite the sentences using a modal of deduction.

items.q: I'm sure she is Brazilian. Listen to her accent.
It's impossible that he wrote this. He can't spell.
Perhaps they took the wrong road.
items.a: They might have taken the wrong road.

items.q: I'm sure the dog was barking all night. Look at the neighbours!
items.a: The dog must have been barking all night.
