story.title: The Cutting Table
story.subtitle: A year of letters, lies and second chances in Lisbon
story.blurb: Every year, on the last day of September, an envelope from England arrives for Marta's grandmother: no name, no letter, just a pressed red flower. This year there is a letter inside, and her grandmother burns it. What survives in the sink is half a sentence, a name nobody in the family has said for fifty years, and an instruction: look under the cutting table.

characters.name: Marta Matos
characters.desc: is sixteen and lives with her grandmother above an old tailor's shop in the Mouraria, Lisbon. Her mother works as a nurse in Luxembourg. She is curious, stubborn and bad at keeping her opinions to herself.

characters.name: Dona Lurdes
characters.desc: is Marta's grandmother, a retired seamstress of sixty-eight with a sharp tongue and a long memory. She keeps her secrets the way she keeps her scissors: close and very sharp.

characters.name: Rafiq Ahmed
characters.desc: is seventeen, was born in Bangladesh and has lived in the flat above Marta's for five years. He works evenings in his uncle's mini-market and wants to be an engineer.

characters.name: Bia Lemos
characters.desc: is Marta's best friend, funny, generous and permanently on her phone. Her father works for the company that wants to buy Marta's building.

characters.name: Mr Okafor
characters.desc: is the new English teacher, on a one-year exchange from Leicester, England. He seems to know more than he says.

characters.name: Rui Fonseca
characters.desc: is Lurdes's nephew, who has just inherited the building from his father. He is charming, nervous and in debt.

chapters.title: The Envelope from Leicester
paragraphs: On the first morning of the school year, Marta was woken by the smell of onions and the sound of her grandmother arguing with the radio.
"Liars," Dona Lurdes told the news. "Every one of them."

Marta lay still and listened to the street. Rua dos Cavaleiros was never quiet. Somebody was rolling up the metal shutter of a shop, somebody else was shouting in Bengali from a balcony, and a tuk-tuk full of tourists was climbing the hill like an old dog that had been asked to do too much. In the Mouraria, it is said, you can hear ten languages before breakfast. In the kitchen, her grandmother was standing at the cooker in her blue housecoat, sixty-eight years old and as straight as a pair of tailor's scissors. On the table lay a white envelope with a green logo: TAGUS LIVING, PREMIUM URBAN HOMES.
"Another one?" Marta asked.
"Read it, if you want to lose your appetite."

Marta read it. The language was polite in the way a knife is polite while it is still in the drawer. It was understood, the letter said, that the building had recently changed hands. It was expected that the new owners would make a generous offer to all residents. It was hoped that an agreement could be reached "in a friendly and efficient manner".
"Who wrote this? A robot?"
"A robot with a lawyer," said Lurdes. "Eat your eggs."

The building had belonged to Lurdes's older brother, Tó, until he died the winter before. Now it belonged to his son, Rui, a nervous man of fifty in expensive trainers who called her "Tia Lurdes" in a voice that always sounded as if he was about to borrow money. On the ground floor was the old tailor's shop, Alfaiataria Fonseca, closed for ten years, its window grey with dust, a headless dummy still wearing half a jacket. Above the shop lived Lurdes and Marta. Above them lived the Ahmed family from Bangladesh, and on the top floor four Nepalese cooks who worked in four different restaurants and were never awake at the same time.
"Rui wouldn't sell it," Marta said. "Not with you inside."
Her grandmother turned off the gas. "I wish you were right," she said, and that was all she said.

Marta's school was a fifteen-minute walk away, down past the mosque on Rua do Benformoso, past the mini-markets selling mangoes and phone chargers, the barbers, the shop that displayed saris next to Benfica shirts. She had grown up here, and she knew which café had the best pastéis de nata.
Her best friend, Bia, was waiting at the school gate with two coffees and the face of someone carrying breaking news.
"New English teacher," Bia said. "British. Very tall. Apparently he once ran a marathon across a desert."
"Says who?"
"Everyone. It's widely believed." Bia handed her a coffee. "Also, your neighbour is in our class this year. The quiet one."
"Rafiq? I thought he was in 12.º."
"He lost a year when he arrived. Something about papers."

Rafiq Ahmed was already sitting in the back row when they walked in, his long legs folded under a desk that was too small for him, reading a library book about bridges. He lived in the flat directly above Marta's. In five years, they had exchanged perhaps two hundred words, most of them "Bom dia" on the stairs. She knew that he worked evenings in his uncle's mini-market and that his mother left the building before six every morning. He presumably knew that Marta lived with her grandmother and that her mother worked in Luxembourg. That was the kind of neighbours they were.

The new teacher arrived at ten past eight, which, everyone agreed later, was very un-British of him. He was tall, Black, about thirty-five, and he wore a grey jacket that fitted him so perfectly that Marta, who had grown up among sewing machines, noticed the jacket before she noticed the man.

"Good morning. I'm Daniel Okafor. I'm from Leicester, which is in the middle of England and which nobody in Portugal has ever heard of." He wrote it on the board. "It's pronounced 'Lester'. Don't ask me why. English spelling was invented to punish foreigners."
People laughed. At the back, Rafiq smiled without looking up from his book.

"This year," Mr Okafor went on, "we're going to talk about a world of many cultures. Migration. Minorities. Who belongs where, and who gets to decide. I'm not going to give you a textbook for that. I'm going to give you a project." Under LEICESTER he wrote two words: ARRIVALS and DEPARTURES. "In pairs, you'll interview someone whose life has been changed by migration. Someone who came here, or someone who left. Then you'll write their story, properly, in English. Not a list of facts. A story."
"Can we choose our partners?" Bia asked hopefully.
"No." He picked up a list. "Beatriz Lemos with Tomás Vaz." Bia groaned. "Marta Matos with Rafiq Ahmed."
Marta turned round. Rafiq had finally lifted his eyes from the book.
"We live in the same building," she said, as if that explained something.
"I know," he said. "I've lived there for five years."

They agreed to meet on Saturday to plan the interviews. They didn't. Rafiq texted on Friday night: "Sorry. Working. Sunday?" On Sunday it rained, and Marta's mother called from Luxembourg: Sofia asking whether Marta was eating properly, Marta asking when she was coming home, both of them pretending not to hear the answer.
"If only the hospitals in Lisbon paid like the ones here," her mother sighed. "I'd be on the next plane."
"You always say that."
"Because it's always true, filha."

Sofia was a nurse. In Luxembourg she earned far more than she had ever earned in Lisbon, and she sent half of it home. Marta understood the arithmetic. She just didn't understand why the arithmetic had to live in her house, in the empty chair at the end of the table.

Every year, on the last day of September, an envelope arrived for her grandmother. It was always the same: a small white envelope with a British stamp, a postmark that said LEICESTER, and no sender's address. Inside, there was never a letter. There was only a red hibiscus flower, pressed flat and dry between two sheets of tissue paper, as thin as the skin on hot milk. When Marta was little, she had believed the flowers came from a secret admirer. Her grandmother always said, "Some old customer. Tailors have customers everywhere," and put the flower inside the same heavy book on the shelf, a Portuguese dictionary that nobody ever opened for any other reason.
This year, Marta stood in the hallway with the envelope in her hand and read the postmark twice. Leicester. Which nobody in Portugal has ever heard of.

The envelope was thicker than usual. Lurdes opened it at the kitchen table with her tailor's scissors, slowly, the way she did everything. Under the flower, folded into four, was a sheet of writing paper.

Marta watched her grandmother read it. She had seen Lurdes angry, bored, amused and once, at Grandpa Fernando's funeral, broken. She had never seen her afraid. Lurdes read the letter to the end, then read it again. Her lips moved without a sound. Then she stood up, took the box of matches from beside the cooker and held the paper over the sink until it caught fire.
"Avó! What are you doing?"

"It's time I stopped keeping rubbish," said Lurdes. She turned on the tap, put the flower in her apron pocket instead of the dictionary, and went to her room. The door closed with a small, final click.

Marta waited until she heard the radio come on behind the door. Then she looked into the sink. Most of the letter was black and wet. One corner had survived, brown at the edges. The words were in Portuguese, in a careful, old-fashioned hand, the hand of someone who had learned to write at a school desk with an inkwell:
"...never took the money, Lurdes. Tó told me everything before he died. Look under the cutting table, he said, and you will..."
That was where the fire had stopped.

Marta did not sleep much that night. At ten past two, she was lying awake, holding the burnt corner and listening to the old building breathe, when she heard a sound from below. A drawer. Then another. A thin light was moving across the wet street outside, the kind of light that comes from a torch held low, and it was coming from the window of the shop.

She went to her grandmother's room. Lurdes was asleep, one hand under her cheek like a child's. In the hallway, the key to the shop was hanging on its nail by the door, where it had hung for ten years.
Downstairs, someone was opening drawers.

chapters.title: Under the Cutting Table
paragraphs: Marta took the only weapon she could find, a pair of her grandmother's iron scissors as long as her forearm, and went down the stairs barefoot.
On the first landing, she walked straight into someone coming up.
They both screamed, not very loudly. Then a phone lit up Rafiq's face. He smelled of cardboard boxes and cumin.
"What are you doing?" he whispered.
"Someone's in the shop."
He looked at the scissors, then at her pyjamas, which had small penguins on them. To his credit, he did not comment on either. "Did you call the police?"
"And say what? That someone is opening drawers?"
"That's usually how burglaries start," he said, but he followed her.

The door from the hallway into the shop was half open. Its lock had not been broken. It had been opened neatly, the way a key opens things. The torch was at the back, near the huge oak cutting table where Marta's great-uncle had once cut suits for lawyers and ministers. Somebody in a dark hoodie was kneeling under it, working with a screwdriver.
Rafiq switched on his phone light and shouted in a voice Marta had never heard him use, deep and furious: "Quem está aí?"

The figure jumped, hit its head on the table, swore in perfect Portuguese and ran. It went out through the back door into the courtyard, over the wall, and was gone. Something small and metallic rolled across the floor and stopped against Marta's bare foot.
It was a pen. A heavy silver one, the kind of pen nobody buys for themselves. Two letters were engraved on the side: R.V.

Five minutes later, every light in the building was on. Lurdes came down in her coat, over her nightdress, and walked straight past the open drawers and the patterns scattered on the floor without looking at them. She went to the cutting table and ran her hand along its edge, as if it were a horse that had been frightened.
"Did they touch it?" she asked.
Rafiq glanced at Marta. "They were trying to take the legs off."
"No police," said Lurdes.
"Avó, someone had a key!"

"No police. The police in this street come when they feel like it, and when they do come, they look at everyone except the thief." She looked at Mrs Ahmed as she said it, and Mrs Ahmed lowered her eyes, and Marta understood that this was a conversation the two women had already had without her.
Rafiq walked Marta back to her door. On the landing, he said quietly, "Did you notice? She didn't ask what was stolen. Only whether they touched the table."
Marta said nothing. The burnt corner of the letter was in the pocket of her penguin pyjamas, and suddenly it felt heavier than the scissors.

In October, the project started properly. Mr Okafor wanted the interviews recorded, transcribed and translated, and he wanted, he said, "the story underneath the story". Rafiq and Marta decided to interview each other's families.
Rafiq interviewed Lurdes in the kitchen, in Portuguese, with his phone on the table. He was good at it. He asked short questions and let the silences be long.

Lurdes told him that she had come to Lisbon in 1971, aged fourteen, from a village near Bragança, with one suitcase and a cardboard box tied with string. "In the village, it was said that the streets of Lisbon were paved with gold. They were paved with stones, and I was the one who swept them." She told him about the shop in its golden years: doctors, lawyers, a minister, an opera singer. She laughed, which she did not often do.
"And who worked here with you?" Rafiq asked.

"My brother. Me. And a cutter." Lurdes stirred the soup, which didn't need stirring. "The best cutter in Lisbon. He was from Cape Verde. He was said to be able to measure a man just by watching him walk past the window."
"What was his name?"
"I don't remember."
Marta, sitting by the window, looked up. Her grandmother still remembered the phone number of a bakery that had closed in 1989.

Marta's interview with Nasreen Ahmed took place a week later, in the Ahmeds' small, tidy flat, under a photograph of green hills covered in tea bushes. Nasreen spoke slow, correct Portuguese and fast, beautiful English, and she preferred English.

She had been a biology teacher in Sylhet. Now she cleaned offices in Parque das Nações from five until nine every morning, and a dentist's surgery in the afternoons. She talked about the queues for residence permits, about arriving at four in the morning to stand in the cold outside an office that gave out twenty appointments a day. She talked about how people spoke to her slowly and loudly, as if her headscarf made her deaf.

"I wish I could teach again," she said. "I wish somebody would look at my diploma before they look at my scarf. But my daughter speaks Portuguese like a little lisboeta, and Rafiq will be an engineer. So." She opened her hands. "It was a fair exchange. Probably."
From the sink, where he was washing up with his back to them, Rafiq said in English, "I'd rather you didn't put the cleaning in the project."
On the stairs afterwards, Marta stopped him. "Why not? It's true."

"Because it's the only thing anyone ever writes about people like us. Cleaners, shopkeepers, delivery riders. That's the whole story, every time." He was angrier than she had ever seen him. "My mother knows the Latin name of every tree in the Jardim da Estrela. Did you know that? Nobody ever asks."
Marta thought about it. "Then that's what I'll write," she said. "If you show me the trees."
He looked at her for a moment, as if he were measuring her again. "Fine," he said. "Saturday."

They went to the Estrela on Saturday. They also went, that same afternoon, into the shop, because Lurdes was at her friend Amélia's playing cards, because the key was on its nail, and because Marta had finally shown Rafiq the burnt corner of the letter.
"Look under the cutting table," he read. "Well. Somebody else knew about this. Before the letter came."

He got down on the floor with his phone light and a tape measure. He measured the drawer under the table, then the table itself, and frowned. "The drawer is forty centimetres deep. The table is fifty-two. There are twelve centimetres missing."
"You're unbearable," said Marta.

"I'm going to be an engineer," said Rafiq, and pushed against the back of the empty drawer space. Something clicked. A thin wooden panel slid sideways, and behind it, wrapped in a piece of grey suit cloth, was an old biscuit tin.

Inside, tied together with a yellow tape measure, was a pile of letters. Twenty-three of them. All addressed to Menina Lurdes Fonseca, Rua dos Cavaleiros, Lisboa. French stamps on the first ones, British stamps on the rest. Postmarks from 1975 to 1979. Every single one of them still sealed.

Under the letters was a photograph. Three young people in front of the shop window: a girl laughing with her head thrown back, so that it took Marta a second to recognise her grandmother; a tall young Black man in a white shirt with a tape measure around his neck, looking at the girl instead of the camera; and at the edge of the picture, half cut out of it, a stiff young man in a suit whom Marta knew at once. Her grandfather, Fernando. On the back, in pencil: Abril de 1975.

And at the very bottom of the tin there was one more envelope. It was not addressed to Lurdes. It was addressed, in Lurdes's own round handwriting, to Sr. José Varela, at an address in Paris. It had a stamp. It had never been posted.
"Put that down."

Lurdes was standing in the doorway, still holding her handbag. She did not shout. She walked across the shop, took the tin out of Marta's hands and sat down heavily on the old stool by the sewing machine. With her thumbnail, she opened the first letter. She read it. Then the second. Rafiq moved quietly towards the door, but Marta could not move at all.
"Tó kept them," Lurdes said at last. "Fifty years. My own brother."
"Avó, who is he? José Varela?"

"Zé," said Lurdes. "His name was Zé." She put the letters back in the tin, every one, and the photograph, and last of all the envelope in her own handwriting, which she held for a long moment before she closed the lid. Then she looked at Marta with an expression Marta had never seen on her face before.
"Listen to me. Your mother must never know about this. Never. Promise me."

chapters.title: The Witness
paragraphs: Marta didn't promise. She didn't say anything at all, and Lurdes took the silence as a yes, or decided to.

After that, the biscuit tin disappeared into Lurdes's bedroom, and something changed in the flat, although it was hard to say exactly what. Lurdes still argued with the radio. She still made soup on Mondays and cleaned the windows on Thursdays. But at night, through the wall, Marta sometimes heard paper: the small, dry sound of a page being turned, then a long silence, then another page.

"You can't ask her," Rafiq said. They were sitting on the steps of the Largo da Achada after school, sharing a paper cone of roasted chestnuts. November had arrived with its smoke and its rain. "They're her letters. It's her story."
"It's my family."
"That's what everyone says when they want to read someone else's post."
Marta threw a chestnut shell at him. But she didn't ask.

Meanwhile, the building had other problems. At the beginning of December, every tenant received the same registered letter. The sale of the building to Tagus Living was now "expected to be completed in the spring". Residents were invited to a meeting with the company's relocation consultant to discuss "compensation and transition solutions".

"Transition solutions," said Bishal, the oldest of the Nepalese cooks, reading it aloud in the shop, where the tenants had gathered on a Sunday afternoon among the dusty dummies. "This means: goodbye."

Everyone had come. Lurdes sat at the cutting table like a judge. Rafiq's father, Kamal, a quiet man with an engineer's careful hands, stood by the wall with Nasreen. The four cooks shared two chairs. Rui had been invited and had not come. He had sent a message saying he was "very busy but completely available to talk".

"Where do we go?" Kamal asked. "I'll tell you what happens when I look for a flat. I phone. The woman says, 'Yes, it's available.' I say my name. Suddenly it has been rented this morning. Every time. It is always rented this morning."
"But that's discrimination," said Marta. "It's illegal."

"Many things are illegal," said Kamal, smiling sadly. "I pay my taxes. I pay social security. I have lived on this street for six years. But I cannot vote for the people who decide what happens to it. My citizenship application has been 'under analysis' for two years. Maybe they are analysing my soul."
Nasreen touched his arm, and he stopped.

Marta looked around the room: the cooks who fed half the tourists in Lisbon, Nasreen who cleaned the offices where decisions were made, her grandmother who had once made suits for ministers. All of them waiting for someone in a glass building to decide where they would live. It's time somebody did something, she thought. If only I were eighteen. If only I knew what to do.
The person who did something, in the end, was Bia, though not in the way anyone expected.

It happened at the school's Christmas fair, between the stall selling cupcakes and the one selling second-hand books. Bia had been strange for weeks: late, distracted, unusually quiet in the group chat. Now she pulled Marta behind the gym and said, very fast, "I need to tell you something and you have to let me finish."
"Okay."
"My dad works for Tagus Living. He's the director of acquisitions. Your building is on a list on his desk. I saw it in October and I didn't say anything, because I thought it would go away."
Marta stared at her. Bia, who lived in Campo de Ourique in a flat with a view of the river. Bia, who had slept at Lurdes's flat a hundred times and eaten a thousand bowls of her soup.
"I'd rather you had told me in October," Marta said at last, and her voice came out colder than she meant it to.
"I know. I wish I'd never seen it." Bia's eyes filled with tears. "He's not a bad person, Marta. He just thinks buildings are numbers."
"My grandmother isn't a number."
"I know that! Why do you think I'm telling you?"

They didn't speak for the rest of the fair. That evening, Bia sent a message with no words, only a photograph: a page from a notebook with a name written on it. Ricardo Vidal. Relocation consultant. Underneath she had added: "Don't know if this helps. He's the one who talks to the tenants. He's very proud of his pen."
Marta took the silver pen out of her desk drawer and turned it in the light. R.V.

Her mother came home on the twenty-second of December, thinner than in the summer and smelling of airports. Sofia was forty-nine, warm and loud, with dark curly hair that nobody else in the family had. "Your grandfather's grandmother was from the Algarve," Lurdes had always explained. "Very dark. Like a Moor." Marta had heard that sentence all her life without ever thinking about it. This Christmas, she noticed that her grandmother watched Sofia across the table in a way she had never noticed before: carefully, as if Sofia were a letter she was afraid to open.

On Christmas Eve, Lurdes invited the Ahmeds for the consoada. Nobody was quite sure how this had happened. Nasreen arrived with a tray of pitha, little rice cakes filled with coconut and palm sugar, and a pot of chicken curry, "because fish on the most important night of the year is a punishment". Kamal and Sofia discovered that they had both worked nights for years in other people's countries, and talked about it, laughing, with the particular laughter of people who have been very tired for a long time. Tania, Rafiq's little sister, taught Lurdes a Bengali song. Lurdes taught Tania to cheat at cards.
Marta and Rafiq ended up on the small balcony, in the cold, with plates of bolo-rei they didn't want.
"It's time you told me what you're planning," Rafiq said. "You've had that face all evening."
"What face?"
"The face you had before you went down to the shop with a pair of scissors."
So she told him. If her grandmother wouldn't talk, there must be other people who could. If a man had been accused of taking money in 1975, perhaps someone had written about it.

The Hemeroteca, the city's newspaper library, opened again on the twenty-ninth. It is not, it must be said, a glamorous place. It smells of dust and silence, and the librarian, a man with a beard like a bird's nest, looked at two teenagers asking for newspapers from 1975 as if they had asked him for a cigarette.
But he helped. It took them three hours and two headaches. Then Rafiq, scrolling through the crime columns of June 1975, stopped and put his finger on the screen.

THEFT IN MOURARIA TAILOR'S SHOP. A large sum of money is reported to have been stolen from the safe of a tailor's shop in Rua dos Cavaleiros. The owner, Mr António Fonseca, informed the police that the money disappeared on the night of 3 June. An employee, José Varela, 22, born in Cape Verde, is believed to have fled the country. It is understood that the theft was witnessed by a neighbour, Mr Fernando Matos, 24, who stated that he had seen the employee leaving the shop with a metal box.
Marta read the last name three times.

Fernando Matos had taught her to ride a bicycle in the Jardim da Estrela. He had peeled oranges for her in one long spiral and called her "minha princesa", and he had died when she was ten, holding her hand.
He was her grandfather. And he had told the police that he had seen Zé Varela steal.

chapters.title: Things We Throw Away
paragraphs: She showed her grandmother the photocopy on the first Sunday of January. She had practised what to say for a week, and in the end she said none of it. She just put the paper on the kitchen table, between the salt and the bread.
Lurdes put on her glasses and read it. She did not seem surprised.
"Where did you find this?"
"At the Hemeroteca. Avó, Grandpa said he saw..."

"I know what Fernando said." Lurdes took off her glasses and folded them very carefully. "He was twenty-four. My brother wrote the statement and Fernando signed it. He didn't see anything. He believed Tó, because Tó was his friend, and because it was easy to believe. A Black man and an open safe, in 1975. It was the easiest story in Lisbon. Everybody believed it. I believed it."
"You believed Zé was a thief?"

"I believed he had left me. That was worse." She looked out of the window. "I stopped blaming Fernando a long time ago. He married me that August, when I needed someone to marry me, and he spent the rest of his life trying to deserve it. Remember that, when you think about him. Remember the oranges."
Marta wanted to ask why her grandmother had needed someone to marry her in August 1975. She didn't. Something in Lurdes's face had closed, like a shop at lunchtime.
"Did you read them? All the letters?"

"I stopped reading after the fifth one. I couldn't go on." Lurdes almost smiled. "Then one night I stopped to make a coffee, and I went on to read the other eighteen before the sun came up. He wrote to me for four years, Marta. Every month. Asking me why I never answered." She stood up. "Now go. Your friend is waiting downstairs, and the soup won't make itself."

School had started again with a new unit, which Mr Okafor and the Geography teacher, Professora Helena, were teaching together. It was called "The Price of a T-shirt", and in the first lesson they emptied a black rubbish bag full of clothes onto the classroom floor.
"These were all thrown away last week," said Professora Helena. "By people in this school. We asked the cleaners to save them for us."
There were jeans with a broken zip. A jumper with one small hole in the elbow. A dress with the price label still on it. Bia went slightly pink and became very interested in her pencil case.

Mr Okafor showed them photographs of a market in Accra, in Ghana, where bales of second-hand clothes from Europe and North America arrive every week, and where much of what arrives cannot be sold and ends up on rubbish dumps and beaches. Then Professora Helena put up a photograph of a collapsed building.
"Does anyone know what this is?"

"Rana Plaza," said Rafiq, before anyone else could answer. "Near Dhaka. 2013. It was a building full of garment factories, and it collapsed. More than a thousand people died." He said it flatly, like a fact from a textbook, but Marta saw his hand tighten around his pen. "My cousin works in a factory like that. She makes jeans for a shop in the Colombo. I've seen them there. Nineteen euros ninety-nine."
For a while, nobody said anything.
"So what are we supposed to do?" Tomás Vaz asked finally. "Stop buying clothes? Walk around naked?"

"You could try mending them," said Marta, and was surprised to hear her own voice. "My grandmother used to repair everything. Coats, trousers, wedding dresses. People didn't throw things away. They had them fixed."
"Nobody gets things fixed anymore," said Bia. "It's cheaper to buy new ones."
"That is exactly the problem," said Mr Okafor, and wrote on the board: WHY HAVE IT REPAIRED WHEN YOU CAN HAVE IT REPLACED? "Discuss."
By the end of the lesson, they had a plan. By the end of the week, Marta had persuaded her grandmother, which was harder.
"A repair café," said Lurdes, as if Marta had suggested opening a nightclub. "In my brother's shop. With teenagers."
"On Saturday mornings. People bring clothes, you show us how to mend them. We learn, they don't throw things away, and the planet says thank you."

"The planet," said Lurdes, "has never once said thank you to me." But she was looking at the old Singer machine in the corner of the kitchen, the one she had stopped using ten years ago, when her eyes began to tire. "I remember teaching your mother to sew on a button. She was six. She sewed it to her own skirt."
"So that's a yes?"
"It's a 'nobody touches my scissors'."

The problem was the key. Rui had had the locks changed after the break-in, without telling anyone, and when Marta phoned him, he sighed as if she had asked him for a kidney. But he came round the next evening, smelling of cologne and stress, and gave Lurdes a new key.

"Until March, Tia. Then Tagus wants to get the whole building renovated before the summer. You understand. It's business." He looked around the shop, at the dummies and the patterns and the great oak table, and something passed over his face, too fast to name. "My father loved this place, you know. He never stopped talking about it."
"Your father," said Lurdes, "talked about many things."

The first Saturday, eleven people came. Dona Amélia brought her late husband's winter coat, which she wanted shortened so she could wear it herself. Bishal brought his chef's jacket, burnt on one sleeve. Tomás brought six pairs of socks with holes in the heels, which Lurdes looked at with such contempt that he took them home again. Mr Okafor came too, with a pair of trousers that needed a new zip, and stayed two hours learning to sew it in himself.
Lurdes sat at the cutting table with her glasses on the end of her nose, and at first she only gave instructions. By eleven o'clock, she had a needle in her hand. By twelve, she was laughing.

"You're holding that needle like a fork," she told Rafiq, who had turned up at half past ten with his little sister's school bag and a broken strap. "Again. Slowly. A tailor who rushes ends up doing everything twice."
"My grandfather used to say that," said Bishal, from the corner. "About cooking."

"Your grandfather was a sensible man." Lurdes held up Dona Amélia's coat, now two hands shorter, and helped her into it. Dona Amélia looked at herself in the long, spotted mirror for a long time without saying anything. Then she put her hands in the pockets, as her husband used to, and burst into tears, and everyone pretended to be very busy with their buttons.
Marta was sewing a patch onto a pair of jeans when she noticed that her grandmother had stopped talking.

Lurdes was looking out of the window, across the street, at the little café on the corner. At one of the tables outside sat an old man. He was Black, thin, very upright, with short white hair, and he was wearing a camel-coloured coat so beautifully made that it seemed to belong to another century. He was not drinking his coffee. He was looking at the shop.
The scissors fell out of Lurdes's hand and hit the floor with a sound like a bell.

She was out of the door before anyone could stop her, crossing the street in her slippers, a tape measure still around her neck. A tuk-tuk braked hard and the driver shouted something. Lurdes didn't hear him.
When she reached the café, the table was empty. The coffee was still warm. Next to the cup, on the white saucer, someone had left a small red flower, pressed flat and dry, as thin as paper.

chapters.title: Made to Measure
paragraphs: "It wasn't him," Lurdes said that night. It was the only thing she would say. "Old men in coats all look the same."

But she did not sleep, and neither did Marta, and on Monday morning the pressed flower was not in the Portuguese dictionary with the others. It was standing in a glass of water on the kitchen windowsill, as if water could bring it back to life.
The waiter at the corner café, a young Brazilian called Wesley, remembered the old man very well.

"He came three mornings in a row. Always the same table, always a coffee he didn't drink. Very polite. Spoke Portuguese like the old Cape Verdean grandfathers, you know, soft, like a song. He asked me how long the tailor's shop had been closed." Wesley shrugged. "I told him it opened on Saturdays now. So on Saturday he came back."
"Did he say where he was staying?"
"No. But he asked me where he could still eat a proper cachupa around here. I sent him to Dona Celeste."

Dona Celeste's restaurant was three streets away: a narrow room with six tables, a television showing a football match from Cape Verde, and a smell of beans, corn and smoked sausage that made Rafiq close his eyes. Dona Celeste herself was large, seventy-five years old, and wore gold earrings the size of coins. She listened to Marta's question, looked her up and down, and sat down at their table without being asked.
"You're the granddaughter. Lurdes's." It was not a question. "You have her chin. God help you."

She had known Zé. Everybody of her generation had known Zé. "He had golden hands. He could take a cheap jacket and make it look like a minister's. And honest, mamã, honest like bread. If you dropped a coin, Zé would run after you down the street to give it back. When they said he had stolen from the Fonsecas, nobody here believed it. Nobody. But who listens to us?"
"Then why did he run away?" Rafiq asked. "If he was innocent?"
Dona Celeste looked at him for a long moment. "You're not from here either, are you, filho?"
"Bangladesh."

"Then you'll understand. That summer, Cape Verde became independent. Good. We wanted it. But a new law came out, and overnight, people like Zé, born over there, living and working here, were no longer Portuguese. Just like that. Foreigners in the city where they paid their rent. Now imagine a foreigner with a police report saying he stole money from a white man's safe. With a witness." She shook her head. "Zé didn't run because he was guilty. He ran because he knew exactly what would happen to him if he stayed. He crossed into Spain at night, then France, on foot, the same way thousands of Portuguese boys had crossed a few years before to escape the war in Africa. Then England. He never came back."
"He came back in January," said Marta.

Dona Celeste was quiet. Then she said, "He stayed with my cousin in Amadora. Ten days. He asked about Lurdes. Whether she was well. Whether she was happy." She hesitated, as if deciding how much to give away. "He has gone back to England now. He's having an operation. On his heart. He wanted to see this street once more before they opened him up, he said. Just in case." She smiled a little. "He was wearing a camel coat. He told my cousin he'd had it made forty years ago, by himself, and had never once had it altered. That's Zé. He always cut for the future."
On the walk home, neither of them spoke for a long time.
"An operation," Marta said at last. "What if he doesn't..."
"Then your grandmother needs to know he came," said Rafiq. "She saw him, Marta. She ran across the street in her slippers."
Meanwhile, without anyone planning it, the repair café had become famous.

It was Bia's fault. She and Marta had made up in January, awkwardly, with a lot of apologising on both sides and a large tub of ice cream. Since then Bia had been coming on Saturdays to film, "for the project". She filmed Lurdes's hands turning a torn sleeve into something better than new. She filmed Dona Amélia walking down Rua dos Cavaleiros in her husband's shortened coat, like a film star. She filmed Tomás learning to darn a sock after all, with an expression of deep suffering. She put it all to music and posted it with the caption: "My best friend's grandmother is 68 and she can fix anything. Except the housing market."

By Tuesday, it had been watched more than four hundred thousand times. By Thursday, a television crew was standing in Rua dos Cavaleiros, filming the shop window. By Saturday, the queue went down the street and round the corner, and Rafiq had to set up a booking website in one night, which he did, complaining the whole time.

"This is what progress is supposed to look like," he said at three in the morning, typing. "Technology that helps an old woman keep her shop open. Not technology that helps a fund turn her shop into a breakfast room for tourists."
"Very poetic. Should the button be blue or green?"
"Green. Green means sustainable. Everybody knows that."
Not everybody was happy. On Sunday, Bia arrived at the shop with red eyes.

"My dad saw the video," she said. "He said I'd made him look like a fool in front of the whole company. He said I would regret posting it." She lifted her chin, exactly like Lurdes. "I told him I didn't regret posting it at all. I only regretted not posting it sooner."

There was one more visitor that month whom Marta would remember later. On the last Saturday in February, Mr Okafor came back to the repair café with his grey jacket over his arm. The lining had torn under one sleeve.
"I've had this jacket for ten years," he said, a little embarrassed. "I can't throw it away. It was a present."
Lurdes took it, turned it inside out, and went very still. She ran her thumb along the inside seam, then along a buttonhole, then along the shoulder, the way Marta had seen her read the letters.
"Who made this?"
"A tailor in Leicester. An old family friend."
"He learned in Lisbon, your tailor," said Lurdes quietly. "I only ever knew one person who finished a buttonhole like this."

For a second, Mr Okafor looked like a boy caught with his hand in the biscuit tin. Then he laughed. "There are a lot of tailors in Leicester, Dona Lurdes. It's a city of tailors." He took the jacket back, very gently. "Maybe I'll get it fixed there."

He left soon afterwards. Marta watched him walk down the street and thought about it for the rest of the afternoon, until Rafiq came down from the roof, where he went when he needed to think, and everything else went out of her head.

"My father has made up his mind," he said. "He's tired of flats that are always rented this morning. My uncle in London has found an engineering company that will sponsor a work visa for him. An engineering company, Marta. After all those years behind a counter." He tried to smile and didn't manage it. "In July, we're moving to London. All of us. Me too."

glossary.pt: de um dia para o outro

chapters.title: Smoke
paragraphs: Marta said the wrong thing. She knew it as soon as it left her mouth.
"Well. Good luck."

Rafiq looked at her as if she had slapped him, and went back up to the roof, and for nine days they said nothing to each other except "Bom dia" on the stairs, exactly as before. That was somehow worse than never having talked at all.
"You're an idiot," said Bia, kindly. "You do know that?"
"He's moving to London. What was I supposed to say? 'Please don't go, the repair café needs a web designer'?"
"You could have tried telling him the truth."
"Which is?"
Bia just looked at her, and Marta looked at the floor.
March was the month when everything began to fall apart, slowly at first and then all at once.

First, the water was cut off for three days "for urgent maintenance", although nobody could find out what was being maintained. Then a pair of electricians in Tagus Living overalls turned up with a letter from Rui and spent a whole morning in the shop. "We're getting the wiring checked before the sale," they said. They left behind a fuse box with a new grey cover and a smell of hot plastic. Then the Nepalese cooks found a note under their door, unsigned, in English: "Foreigners with no contract should think about their future." Bishal, who had a contract and had shown it to Marta twice, laughed when he read it. But that night he put a chair under the door handle.

"It's a campaign," said Rafiq. It was the first thing he had said to her in nine days. They were both standing in the hallway, looking at the note, and he seemed to have forgotten that he wasn't talking to her. "They're trying to wear us down. Water, noise, threats. People give up and take the money just to make it stop."
"How do you know?"
"Because my uncle went through exactly the same thing in Arroios two years ago. Same steps. Like a recipe."
"Then we won't give up," said Marta. And then, because it was easier to say it to the note than to his face: "I'm sorry. About 'good luck'. It was a stupid thing to say."
"Yes," he agreed. "It was." But he smiled for the first time in nine days, and for now that was enough.

At school, it was sustainability week, and the 11.º classes had to hold a debate: "Progress: who pays the bill?" Rafiq argued that progress was always paid for by somebody who wasn't in the room: the cousin in the garment factory, the tenants in the old building, the fishermen downstream of the dam. Tomás argued that without progress they would all still be dying of toothache. Mr Okafor said they were both right, which annoyed everybody. Marta argued that a city where the people who cook the food and clean the offices can't afford to live is not progress, it is a postcard. She got a round of applause and an extra mark, and she couldn't concentrate on any of it.

Bia found the last piece of the puzzle by accident. Her father had left his laptop open on the kitchen table, and she had not, she said, been looking. Not really. Not much. There was an email from Ricardo Vidal to her father. It was short. "Rua dos Cavaleiros: pressure measures in progress as agreed. The old lady and the Bangladeshis should come round by April. Shop wiring taken care of."
"Taken care of," said Bia, white-faced, at the shop. "What does 'taken care of' mean?"
"I don't know," said Rafiq, looking at the new grey fuse box. "But I don't like it."

Bia did something then that Marta would admire for the rest of her life. She went home and showed the email to her father. She didn't shout. She put the laptop in front of him and asked one question: "Did you agree to this?"
Henrique Lemos read it twice. Then, Bia told them, he went into his study and didn't come out for three hours, and when he came out, he was on the phone to a lawyer.

"He didn't know," Bia said. "I believe him. He thought Vidal was just offering people money. He said, 'I've never once been to that street.' As if that made it better." She laughed, not happily. "Maybe that's the whole problem. Nobody who makes the decisions has ever been to the street."

But finding something out is not the same as stopping it. At the end of March, Rui signed the promissory contract. The sale would be completed in May. He came to tell Lurdes himself, which Marta thought was either brave or cowardly, and possibly both.
"I'm sorry, Tia. I really am. I've got debts. The business, the divorce. I can't afford to be sentimental."
"Nobody is asking you to be sentimental, Rui," said Lurdes. "Only to be your father's son for once, and not in the way he was."
Rui didn't understand. Marta did, and she held her breath, but her grandmother said nothing more, and Rui left without finishing his coffee.

That night, Marta finally told her grandmother what she had been carrying around since February. She had meant to tell her weeks before, and every evening she had put it off. Now she told her everything: Wesley, the cachupa, Dona Celeste's earrings, the ten days in Amadora, the coat he had never had altered. The heart.
Lurdes listened without interrupting. When Marta got to the operation, she put down the sock she was darning and sat very still, her hands flat on her knees.
"When?"
"Dona Celeste didn't know. Soon, she said. In England."

"Fifty years," said Lurdes, to nobody. "Fifty years he couldn't come, and when he finally comes, I'm sewing a zip into a teacher's trousers." She picked the sock up again, and put it down again. "I'll never forget seeing him at that table. Never. Not if I live to be a hundred. And I didn't even get to see his face properly. Only the coat." Her mouth moved in something that was nearly a smile. "It was a very good coat."
"Avó, if you want to write to him..."

"I tried writing to him once," said Lurdes. "It didn't arrive." She stood up, and the conversation was over, but before she closed her bedroom door she said, without turning round: "Thank you for telling me, filha. Next time, don't wait a month."

That last Saturday of the 2.º período, the repair café had its biggest day ever: ninety people, a journalist from a national newspaper, and a woman from the city council who took a great many notes and asked a great many questions about the building. Lurdes had gone to bed early, exhausted and happy, with flour on her sleeve from the cake Nasreen had brought. Marta fell asleep over her Physics book.
She woke at ten to three with a strange taste in her mouth.
Smoke. Not cigarette smoke. Something heavier, oily, like burning plastic. She was out of bed before she knew it, running to her grandmother's room.
Lurdes's bed was empty. The covers had been thrown back. The biscuit tin was not on the bedside table, where it had been every night since October.
Marta ran into the hallway. The nail by the door was empty too.
Below her, on the ground floor, a thin grey ribbon of smoke was curling out from under the door of the shop.

chapters.title: The Letter in the Tin
paragraphs: Never in her life had Marta moved so fast.

Afterwards, she remembered only pieces: her own voice screaming Rafiq's name up the stairwell; the heat of the door handle through her pyjama sleeve; the door opening onto a wall of black smoke that made her eyes stream. Rafiq was beside her before she had finished screaming, with Bishal behind him holding a wet towel, and somebody upstairs was already on the phone to 112.

They found Lurdes on the floor beside the cutting table, where the smoke was thinnest. She was conscious but confused, coughing, holding the biscuit tin against her chest with both arms like a baby. Flames were climbing the wall behind the fuse box, licking at the old paper patterns pinned there. Rafiq and Bishal lifted her between them. Marta took the tin, because her grandmother would not let go of it for anyone else.
No sooner had they reached the street than the shop window cracked with a sound like a gunshot.

The firefighters arrived a few minutes later. Hardly had they begun unrolling the hoses when the whole street was awake: the Ahmeds in their coats, Dona Amélia from across the road with a rosary, Wesley from the café with a tray of water, the tuk-tuk drivers who slept in their vehicles further down the hill. Someone put a blanket around Marta's shoulders. She never found out who.

Lurdes spent five days in the Hospital de São José with smoke in her lungs and a broken wrist. The shop survived, in a way. The back wall was black, the dummies had melted into strange, sad shapes, and the window was boarded up. But the oak cutting table, which had been built, Lurdes said, "in the days when furniture was meant to outlive people", was only scorched.

The investigators were clear. The fire had started in the fuse box. "Someone did work on this installation recently," the fire officer told Marta, "and it can't have been a qualified electrician. No qualified electrician would connect it like that. Whoever did it must have known it was dangerous."
"Could it have been an accident?"
He looked at her. "It might have been. But I'd want to know who sent them."

A lot of people wanted to know. Not only did Henrique Lemos give the police Vidal's emails, but he also resigned from Tagus Living the same week, in a letter that somebody leaked to the newspapers. Never had the Mouraria seen so many television cameras: in the street, outside the hospital, outside Tagus Living's glass offices on the Avenida da Liberdade. By the middle of April, the company announced that it was "withdrawing from the Rua dos Cavaleiros project" and "cooperating fully with the authorities". Ricardo Vidal could not be reached for comment. It came out later that in September he had borrowed Rui's keys "to show the building to investors", and had kept a copy.
"So we won," said Bia, uncertainly.
"Rui still has debts," said Rafiq. "He'll find another buyer. Someone with a nicer pen."

The 3.º período started the following week, and with it came something Marta had completely forgotten: the work experience week in Leicester. Mr Okafor had organised it in the autumn with a college there: ten days in May, eight students, each one placed in a real workplace. Marta had applied in November, when it had seemed like a fun idea. Now it seemed impossible.
"I can't go. Not now. Avó has one hand. Who's going to help her?"
"Your mother," said Lurdes from her hospital bed. "She's coming home on Thursday. And you are going to England, even if I have to carry your suitcase to the airport in my teeth."

First, there were forms to fill in, a CV to write in English, and an interview with the college by video call. Mr Okafor made them practise in class. "Under no circumstances," he said, "should you write that you are 'a hard worker and a team player'. Everybody writes that. It means nothing. Tell me something only you could say."

Rafiq wrote that he had built a booking system for nine hundred customers in one night. Bia wrote that she had once caused a director of acquisitions to resign. Mr Okafor suggested that she might want to rephrase that.

"And in the interview," he went on, "they will probably ask why you want to go. You should have a better answer than 'because it's in England'. You needn't sound perfect. You must sound like yourselves."
"What if they ask something we can't answer?" asked Tomás.
"Then you say so. Nobody has ever been rejected for saying 'I don't know, but I'd like to find out'."

Marta's mother arrived on Thursday, as promised, and took over the flat as if she had never left. In the evenings, with Lurdes asleep, mother and daughter talked in a way they had not talked for years. Marta's class was preparing a debate on the question "Should young Portuguese people go abroad to work?" and she practised her arguments on Sofia.

"On the one hand, you earn more and you learn a lot," Marta said. "On the other hand, you leave everything behind. Moreover, the country trains doctors and nurses and engineers and then loses them. Therefore..."

"Therefore nothing," said Sofia. "It isn't a debate when it's your own life. I went because I had a mortgage and a daughter and a salary that ran out on the twentieth of every month. Although I don't regret going, I regret what it cost. Mainly you." She looked at her hands. "Should the hospital here offer me a decent contract, I'd come back tomorrow. I've told them so."
"Have they answered?"
"Not yet. But your grandmother nearly died, Marta. That changes the arithmetic."

The night before Marta left for Leicester, Lurdes, home again with her arm in plaster, called her into her bedroom. The biscuit tin was on the bed. Its edges were black, and it still smelled of smoke.

"Do you know why I went down to the shop that night?" Lurdes asked. "I had put the tin back in the table, behind the panel. I thought it was the safest place. It had been safe for fifty years." With her good hand, she opened the lid and took out the envelope addressed in her own round handwriting to José Varela in Paris, with its stamp that had never been posted. "I couldn't sleep. I wanted to read this again. I wanted to know if I would still say the same things."
"Would you?"

"Every word." She held out the envelope. "You're going to Leicester. I'm not stupid. I know you'll look for him. If you find him, give him this. It's fifty years late. I'd rather he heard it from me than from anyone else."
"Avó, what does it say?"
"It says what it says. It's not for you to open, filha. Promise me that, at least."
This time, Marta promised.
In the morning, early, before the taxi came, she went to say goodbye to her grandmother again. The bedroom door was half open, and she stopped, because Lurdes was not alone.

Mr Okafor was sitting on the chair beside the bed, holding Lurdes's good hand. He was talking quietly and quickly, and he was speaking Portuguese. Not the careful Portuguese of a foreign teacher on exchange, but soft, musical Portuguese, the kind Wesley had called the Portuguese of the old Cape Verdean grandfathers.
"Ele está a recuperar bem, Dona Lurdes. A operação correu bem. Ele pediu-me para lhe dizer que..."
He's recovering well. The operation went well. He asked me to tell you that...
Marta pushed the door open. Mr Okafor turned round, and the look on his face was the look of a man who had been waiting eight months for this moment and still wasn't ready for it.
"Since when," said Marta, "do you speak Portuguese?"

chapters.title: A City with No Majority
paragraphs: "Since I was born," said Mr Okafor. "My mother is from Cape Verde. She spoke Portuguese to me until I was five, and then she gave up, because I always answered in English. I understand everything. My cousins say I speak like an old woman from Mindelo."
"You let us translate for you. All year. You sat there while I interviewed my own grandmother."

"Marta." It was Lurdes. "I asked him not to tell you. He came to see me in the hospital, after the fire, and I asked him again who had made that jacket. This time he told me the truth, and then I asked him to keep it to himself. Don't be angry with him. Be angry with me. I'm used to it."

There was no time to be angry with anyone. The taxi was hooting in the street, with Bia in it, and Rafiq, and too many suitcases. Mr Okafor picked up his bag. "I'll explain everything in Leicester," he said quietly at the door. "I promise. All of it."

They flew to London on a grey Sunday morning and took the train north from St Pancras. From the window, England looked exactly like the pictures: small green fields with hedges round them, like a quilt Lurdes might have made. Rafiq photographed every bridge. Bia slept with her mouth open. Marta held her backpack on her knees the whole way, with her grandmother's letter in the inside pocket.
Leicester was not like the pictures. Leicester was not like anywhere Marta had ever been.

"Here's a fact for your project," Mr Okafor said on the first evening, as they walked down Belgrave Road past sari shops, sweet shops and jewellers' windows full of gold. "In this city, there is no majority. White British, Indian, Pakistani, Somali, Polish, Caribbean, Bangladeshi... Every group is a minority. Nobody is the main character."
"Does it work?" asked Bia.

Mr Okafor thought about it. "Most days. Not every day. You can't just put people next to each other and call it a success. People need work, and homes, and to feel that nobody is looking down on them. Where they have that, it works quite well. Where they don't, it doesn't work anywhere."

The placements began on Monday. Rafiq went to an engineering firm that designed footbridges, and came back every evening glowing as if someone had plugged him in. Bia went to a law firm that defended tenants in housing cases, "which is either a coincidence or the universe being sarcastic". Marta went to a small workshop near the market called Second Stitch, run by a Polish woman called Agnieszka, which repaired clothes, taught sewing to refugees and sold what they made.

"You must wear these," said Agnieszka on the first morning, giving Marta a pair of thick gloves for the steam press. "You needn't bring lunch, we all eat together. And you should ask if you don't understand something. Here, nobody is born knowing."

Marta liked it immediately. The workshop smelled like her grandmother's shop before the fire. On the second day, she took in a coat for a Syrian man who had been a judge in his own country and now drove a delivery van, and he described the mountains outside his city while she sewed. On the third day, she asked Agnieszka whether she had ever heard of a tailor called Joe Varela.

Agnieszka put down her scissors. "Everybody in this trade has heard of Joe. He was the best. He had a shop near the Clock Tower for forty years. He started in a hosiery factory in the seventies, when this city was full of them. Night shifts. Then he saved and saved and opened his own place." She frowned. "He closed it in November. He said it was time to stop. Then he had a heart operation. I heard it went well, but he's still in the Royal Infirmary. Some kind of complications."
That evening, Marta found Mr Okafor in the lobby of the hostel.
"You promised," she said. "All of it."
They walked to a café near the Clock Tower, and he told her while his tea went cold.

His mother, Fátima, had arrived in Leicester in 1979, nineteen years old and alone. The first person who helped her, who found her a room, a job and a winter coat, was a quiet Cape Verdean tailor who worked nights in a hosiery factory. When Daniel was born, that tailor became his godfather. "Joe was always there. Every birthday. Every school play. He taught me to tie a tie. He made that jacket for my graduation." Mr Okafor smiled. "He never married. My mum used to tease him about it. He said he had been married once, in his heart, in Lisbon, and once was enough."

Last summer, Joe had received a letter from Portugal, from a dying man called António Fonseca. "I'd never seen him cry before. He asked me to read it to him, because his eyes were already bad. Marta, I'm not going to tell you what was in it. It isn't mine to tell. But afterwards he asked me to find out whether Lurdes was well. Just that. Whether she was well. I had already applied to teach abroad for a year. I asked for Lisbon. I asked for the school nearest Rua dos Cavaleiros." He rubbed his face. "Then I read the class list on the first morning, and there you were. Marta Fonseca Matos. I nearly walked out of the room."
"You gave me the project on purpose. Arrivals and departures."

"I gave everyone the project. I paired you with Rafiq because you were the only two people in that class who hadn't spoken to each other in five years, even though you lived in the same building. That was the teacher in me, not the godson." He hesitated. "Should I have told you? Probably. I've asked myself that every week since September. But it wasn't my secret. It was your grandmother's. And his."
"Can I see him?"

"He isn't well, Marta. There were complications. He gets confused, he sleeps a lot. He told me he doesn't want anyone from Lisbon to see him like this." Mr Okafor looked at her, and for once he looked exactly like what he was: a tired man of thirty-five caught between other people's decisions. "I'm sorry. Wait until he's better."

She waited one day. Then, on Thursday afternoon, she told Agnieszka she had a dentist's appointment, which was the worst lie she had ever told, and caught a bus to the Leicester Royal Infirmary. Not until she was standing at the main entrance did she realise that she had no plan at all.

It took her forty minutes to find the right ward, and a nurse with a Ghanaian accent who looked at the envelope in Marta's hand and decided, for reasons she never explained, to help. "Bed six, by the window. He's been asleep most of the day, love. Don't tire him."

He was smaller than she had imagined. In the camel coat, in January, he had seemed tall; in the hospital bed, under the white sheet, he was a thin old man with a drip in his arm and his white hair flat on one side. His hands lay on the blanket. They were long and very clean, with the slight thickening at the fingertips that her grandmother's hands had, the hands of someone who has pushed a needle through cloth a hundred thousand times.

Marta sat down on the plastic chair. She never knew how long she sat there. Ten minutes. An hour. Then the old man opened his eyes and looked at her, and his whole face changed, as if somebody had switched on a light inside it.
"Lurdes?" he whispered.
"No," said Marta, and her voice shook. "I'm her granddaughter. I'm Marta."
He looked at her for a long time: at her chin, at her eyes, at the dark hair that curled the way nobody else's in the family did, except her mother's. Then, slowly, he reached out and took her hand.
"Then you are mine too," said Zé Varela.

chapters.title: Fonseca & Varela
paragraphs: He did not let go of her hand while Marta, in a voice that kept breaking in the wrong places, told him about the envelopes, the burnt corner in the sink, the biscuit tin, the fire. He listened with his eyes closed, nodding very slightly.
When she had finished, she took the envelope out of her backpack.
"She asked me to give you this. She wrote it in 1975. It was never posted."
Zé looked at the round handwriting for a long time without touching it. "Read it to me," he said at last. "My eyes are finished, filha. Fifty years of black thread."
"She told me not to open it."
"She told you not to open it for yourself," said Zé. "This is for me."
So Marta opened it, in a hospital in the middle of England, and read her grandmother's words aloud.

"Zé. I don't know if this will reach you. Celeste says you are in Paris, at this address, and I am going to believe her, because I have to believe something. They say you took the money. I don't believe it. I didn't believe it for one minute, not even when I was angry with you for leaving, not even when Tó shouted and Fernando signed that paper. You are the man who runs down the street to give back a coin. I have to tell you something, and I wish I could say it to your face. I am going to have a baby. Our baby. The doctor thinks it will be born in February. Tell me where you are and I will come. Paris, England, the end of the world. I would rather be poor with you anywhere than comfortable without you here. If you don't answer, I will understand that you can't, and I will do what I have to do. But answer me, Zé. Please answer. Your Lurdes. Lisbon, 10 July 1975."
Marta stopped reading. Somewhere a machine beeped, patiently.

February. Her mother's birthday was the fourteenth of February. Her mother, with the dark curly hair that nobody else in the family had. A grandmother from the Algarve, very dark, like a Moor. Grandpa Fernando, who had married Lurdes in August 1975, "when I needed someone to marry me". Your mother must never know.
Only then did Marta understand what she had carried across Europe in her backpack. Only then did she understand what the old man had meant.
"You knew," she said. "Before I came. You already knew."

"Since last summer." Zé opened his eyes. They were wet, but his voice was steady. "Tó wrote to me before he died. A long letter. Not a brave one, but true, at last. He had debts in 1975. Gambling. Dangerous people. He took the money from the safe himself, and when the police came, he needed a thief. I was the easiest thief in Lisbon. He told Fernando he had seen me with the box, and Fernando, who was young and in love with your grandmother and not very fond of me, believed him and signed." He breathed slowly. "Then the letters started coming. Mine, from Paris and Leicester. And hers, which she gave him to post. He couldn't post them and he couldn't burn them. So he hid them under the table, where he had to see them every day. A coward even in his crimes, poor Tó."
"And in his letter, he told you about my mother."

"He wrote: 'Lurdes's daughter is yours. Fernando knew, and raised her as his own, and was a better father than I was a brother. I took fifty years from you both.'" Zé pressed her hand. "Fifty years, a daughter, and a granddaughter who is sitting in front of me with her grandmother's chin."
"Everyone says that about the chin."
"Everyone is right."

They talked until the nurse sent her away. He told her about the hosiery factory, the night shifts, his first English winter, which he had survived in a coat he had sewn himself out of a blanket. He told her why the flowers came on the last day of September: because on that day in 1973 a sixteen-year-old girl from Trás-os-Montes had opened the door of the Alfaiataria Fonseca to a Cape Verdean boy asking for work, and had told him, with that chin, that he was holding his scissors wrong.
"And the hibiscus?"
"It grew outside my mother's door in Mindelo. Every year I thought, this year she will write back. She never did. So I sent a flower without words. Words had already failed me."
"She didn't know," said Marta. "She thought you had left her."

"I know that now." He smiled, very tiredly. "Had I known then, nothing in this world would have kept me away. But we can't sew the past again, filha. We can only take it in a little, let it out a little, and wear it."

The next afternoon, with Mr Okafor's permission this time, Marta went back to the hospital and made a video call to Lisbon. Lurdes held the phone far too close to her face, as always, so that most of the time all Zé could see was one eye and a lot of forehead.
"You've got old," said Lurdes.
"And you still don't know how to hold a telephone," said Zé.
Then neither of them said anything at all for a long time, and Marta and Mr Okafor looked out of the window and pretended not to cry.

Lurdes did not wait for Marta to come home. That same evening, she sat her daughter down at the kitchen table, between the salt and the bread, and told her everything. Sofia did not speak to her mother for two days. On the third day, she walked alone to Dona Celeste's restaurant, ordered cachupa, ate every bit of it, cried into it, and walked home. "Tell me about him," she said. "From the beginning. And don't you dare leave anything out."

Not all endings are neat, and this one was not. Ricardo Vidal was charged, although the case would take years. Tagus Living changed its name. Rui, who had received a copy of his father's letter from Zé, came to see Lurdes at the end of May and sat in her kitchen for a long time without a word. In the end, he sold the building to the city council, which had started buying old buildings in the centre to rent at fair prices. It is said that the council paid a lot less than Tagus had offered. Rui never said how much, and Lurdes never asked.

The Ahmeds would leave for London in July, as planned. Rafiq would not. His uncle had a spare room above the mini-market, Técnico was in Lisbon, and Lurdes had told Kamal, in a voice that did not allow discussion, that the boy would eat his dinners on the first floor of Rua dos Cavaleiros until he was a qualified engineer. Sofia signed a contract with the Hospital de São José and gave notice in Luxembourg.

On the twelfth of June, the night of Santo António, when the whole of the Mouraria smells of grilled sardines and every balcony is hung with paper garlands, a taxi stopped at the bottom of Rua dos Cavaleiros. An old man got out, slowly, with a walking stick he clearly hated, wearing a camel coat that was far too hot for June. Mr Okafor got out of the other side and pretended not to be ready to catch him.

The shop was waiting. The burnt wall had been painted white. Rafiq and Bishal had sanded the cutting table until it shone. Above the new window, Bia had painted the sign herself, in green: FONSECA & VARELA. REPAIRS, ALTERATIONS, SECOND LIVES.
Lurdes was standing in the doorway, her arm out of plaster. Sofia was behind her. Neither of them moved.
Zé walked up the street to the door. He looked at Lurdes for a long time.
"That coat is too hot for June," said Lurdes.
"I know," said Zé. "It's the only one good enough."

Then he turned to Sofia, and Marta, watching from the steps across the street with Rafiq beside her, saw her mother's face do something she had never seen it do: open, completely, like a window in summer.
"You have her chin," said Zé.
Sofia laughed and cried at the same time. "Everyone says that."
Much later, when the sardines were finished and the music was so loud that the walls seemed to shake, Rafiq asked her what she was going to write for Mr Okafor's project.

Marta looked across the street. Through the new window, in the yellow light of the shop, an old woman was measuring an old man for a summer jacket, and telling him, as she had told him once before, in 1973, that he was holding his scissors wrong.
"The story underneath the story," she said.

reading.title: The Envelope from Leicester
text: On the first morning of the school year, Marta was woken by the smell of onions and the sound of her grandmother arguing with the radio. In the kitchen, Dona Lurdes, sixty-eight years old and as straight as a pair of tailor's scissors, pointed at a white envelope on the table. It came from Tagus Living, a company that sold "premium urban homes".

The language of the letter was polite in the way a knife is polite while it is still in the drawer. It was understood, the letter said, that the building had recently changed hands. It was expected that the new owners would make a generous offer to all residents. It was hoped that an agreement could be reached "in a friendly and efficient manner".

The building had belonged to Lurdes's brother, Tó, until he died the winter before. Now it belonged to his son, Rui, a nervous man who always sounded as if he was about to borrow money. On the ground floor was the old tailor's shop, closed for ten years. Above it lived Lurdes and Marta; above them, the Ahmed family from Bangladesh; and on the top floor, four Nepalese cooks. "Rui wouldn't sell it," Marta said. "Not with you inside." Her grandmother turned off the gas. "I wish you were right," she said.

At school, the new English teacher introduced himself. "I'm Daniel Okafor. I'm from Leicester, which is in the middle of England and which nobody in Portugal has ever heard of." This year, he explained, the class would talk about migration and minorities, and they would do a project: in pairs, they would interview someone whose life had been changed by migration. Marta was paired with Rafiq Ahmed, the quiet boy who lived in the flat above hers. In five years, they had exchanged perhaps two hundred words.

Every year, on the last day of September, an envelope arrived for Lurdes: a British stamp, a postmark that said LEICESTER, no sender's address and, inside, only a pressed red hibiscus flower. Lurdes always said it came from "some old customer". This year, the envelope was thicker. Under the flower there was a letter. Lurdes read it twice, went pale and burned it in the sink. "It's time I stopped keeping rubbish," she said.

One corner survived. In a careful, old-fashioned hand, Marta read: "...never took the money, Lurdes. Tó told me everything before he died. Look under the cutting table..." That night, at ten past two, Marta heard drawers opening in the shop below. Her grandmother was asleep, and the key to the shop was still hanging on its nail by the door.

writing.task: Mr Okafor asks you to write a text for the class blog called **"My street, many cultures"**. Describe a street or neighbourhood you know well and the different people, languages and traditions you find there. Write **120-180 words**.
writing.model: I live in Arroios, in Lisbon, and my street is like a small world. On the corner there is a Chinese supermarket where I buy noodles at midnight, and next to it a Brazilian café that plays samba from eight in the morning. The barber is from Nepal and he cuts hair while he talks about cricket, which I still don't understand. My neighbours upstairs are an old Portuguese couple who have lived here for fifty years. They complain about the noise, but they also give sweets to every child in the building, whatever language the child speaks. It is said that Arroios is one of the most multicultural parts of the city, and I believe it. Of course, it is not perfect. Rents are rising and some families have had to leave. I wish the people who decide about our neighbourhood came here more often. It's time they listened to the people who actually live in it.

reading.title: Under the Cutting Table
text: Marta went down the stairs barefoot, holding her grandmother's heavy iron scissors. On the first landing, she walked straight into Rafiq, who was coming home from his uncle's mini-market at two in the morning. Together, they went down to the shop. The door was half open. Its lock had not been broken: it had been opened neatly, the way a key opens things. At the back, someone in a dark hoodie was kneeling under the big oak cutting table with a screwdriver. When Rafiq shouted, the figure ran out through the back door and over the courtyard wall. It left behind a heavy silver pen with two letters engraved on it: R.V.

Lurdes came down in her coat and walked straight past the open drawers and the patterns on the floor without looking at them. She went to the cutting table. "Did they touch it?" she asked. She refused to call the police. "The police in this street come when they feel like it, and when they do come, they look at everyone except the thief." Later, Rafiq said quietly, "Did you notice? She didn't ask what was stolen. Only whether they touched the table."

In October, the two teenagers started their interviews. Lurdes told Rafiq that she had arrived in Lisbon in 1971, aged fourteen. "In the village, it was said that the streets of Lisbon were paved with gold. They were paved with stones, and I was the one who swept them." She also mentioned a cutter from Cape Verde, the best in Lisbon. But when Rafiq asked his name, she said, "I don't remember." Marta knew that was a lie: her grandmother still remembered the phone number of a bakery that had closed in 1989.

Rafiq's mother, Nasreen, had been a biology teacher in Bangladesh. Now she cleaned offices. "I wish somebody would look at my diploma before they look at my scarf," she told Marta. From the sink, Rafiq said, "I'd rather you didn't put the cleaning in the project. It's the only thing anyone ever writes about people like us."

One Saturday, while Lurdes was out, Rafiq measured the drawer under the cutting table. It was twelve centimetres shorter than the table. He pushed the back of the drawer space, and a panel slid open. Behind it was an old biscuit tin with twenty-three letters addressed to Lurdes, sent from France and Britain between 1975 and 1979. Not one had been opened. There was also an old photograph and one envelope in Lurdes's own handwriting, addressed to a José Varela in Paris. It had never been posted.

Lurdes appeared in the doorway and took the tin. After reading two letters, she said, "Tó kept them. Fifty years. My own brother." Then she turned to Marta. "Your mother must never know about this. Never. Promise me."

reading.title: The Witness
text: At the beginning of December, every tenant received the same registered letter. The sale of the building to Tagus Living was "expected to be completed in the spring". Residents were invited to discuss "compensation and transition solutions". "Transition solutions," said Bishal, one of the Nepalese cooks. "This means: goodbye."

The tenants met in the old shop. Rafiq's father, Kamal, a quiet man with an engineer's careful hands, explained his fear. "When I look for a flat, I phone. The woman says, 'Yes, it's available.' I say my name. Suddenly it has been rented this morning. Every time." He paid his taxes, he said, but he could not vote for the people who decided what happened to his street. "My citizenship application has been 'under analysis' for two years. Maybe they are analysing my soul." Marta looked around the room. It's time somebody did something, she thought. If only I were eighteen.

At the school Christmas fair, Bia pulled Marta behind the gym. "My dad works for Tagus Living. He's the director of acquisitions. Your building is on a list on his desk. I saw it in October and I didn't say anything." Marta's voice came out colder than she meant it to: "I'd rather you had told me in October." Bia's eyes filled with tears. "I wish I'd never seen it. He's not a bad person. He just thinks buildings are numbers." That evening, Bia sent her a name: Ricardo Vidal, relocation consultant. R.V., like the initials on the silver pen.

Marta's mother, Sofia, came home for Christmas. She had dark curly hair that nobody else in the family had, and Marta noticed that Lurdes watched her daughter carefully, "as if Sofia were a letter she was afraid to open". On Christmas Eve, the Ahmeds joined them for dinner, and Nasreen brought rice cakes and a chicken curry, "because fish on the most important night of the year is a punishment".

After Christmas, Marta and Rafiq went to the Hemeroteca, the city's newspaper library. After three hours, they found a short article from June 1975: "A large sum of money is reported to have been stolen from the safe of a tailor's shop in Rua dos Cavaleiros. An employee, José Varela, 22, born in Cape Verde, is believed to have fled the country. It is understood that the theft was witnessed by a neighbour, Mr Fernando Matos, 24."

Marta read the last name three times. Fernando Matos had taught her to ride a bicycle and had peeled oranges for her in one long spiral. He was her grandfather. And he had told the police that he had seen Zé Varela steal.
