reading.title: Things We Throw Away
text: In January, Marta showed her grandmother the newspaper article. Lurdes did not seem surprised. "My brother wrote the statement and Fernando signed it. He didn't see anything. He believed Tó, because it was easy to believe. A Black man and an open safe, in 1975. It was the easiest story in Lisbon." She had stopped blaming Fernando long ago. "He married me that August, when I needed someone to marry me, and he spent the rest of his life trying to deserve it." Marta wanted to ask why. She didn't. Something in Lurdes's face had closed, like a shop at lunchtime.

At school, Mr Okafor and the Geography teacher started a unit called "The Price of a T-shirt". They emptied a bag of clothes that students had thrown away onto the classroom floor: jeans with a broken zip, a jumper with one small hole, a dress with the price label still on it. They showed photographs of a market in Accra, Ghana, where bales of second-hand clothes from rich countries arrive every week, and where much of what arrives cannot be sold. Rafiq talked about Rana Plaza, a building full of garment factories near Dhaka that collapsed in 2013. "My cousin works in a factory like that," he said. "She makes jeans for a shop in the Colombo. Nineteen euros ninety-nine."

"You could try mending them," Marta suggested. "People used to have things fixed." By the end of the week, she had persuaded her grandmother to open a repair café in the old shop on Saturday mornings. "The planet," said Lurdes, "has never once said thank you to me." But she agreed, on one condition: nobody touched her scissors.

Rui had had the locks changed after the break-in, but he came round with a new key. "Until March, Tia. Then Tagus wants to get the whole building renovated before the summer." He looked around the shop. "My father loved this place. He never stopped talking about it." "Your father," said Lurdes, "talked about many things."

On the first Saturday, eleven people came. Dona Amélia brought her late husband's winter coat to have it shortened. Lurdes only gave instructions at first, but by twelve o'clock she was laughing, a needle in her hand.

Then she stopped talking. Across the street, at the café on the corner, sat an old Black man in a beautifully made camel-coloured coat. He was not drinking his coffee. He was looking at the shop. The scissors fell from Lurdes's hand. She ran across the street in her slippers, but when she reached the café, the table was empty. On the saucer lay a small red flower, pressed flat and dry.

writing.task: Write an **article for the school magazine** with the title **"Repair it, don't replace it"**. Persuade other students to repair their clothes instead of throwing them away. Give reasons and practical ideas. Write **120-180 words**.
writing.model: Last week our class emptied a bag of clothes onto the classroom floor. Everything in it had been thrown away by students from this school, and almost everything could have been saved: a jacket with a missing button, jeans with a broken zip, a jumper with one tiny hole. Cheap clothes are not really cheap. Somebody pays for them, usually a badly paid worker far away, and the planet pays when they end up in a rubbish dump. So before you throw something away, stop to think. Could you mend it yourself? Sewing on a button takes five minutes, and there are hundreds of videos online. If you can't do it, have it repaired. A small alteration at a local tailor's costs less than a new T-shirt and keeps a neighbourhood shop alive. You can also swap clothes with friends or come to our repair café on Saturday mornings. Your favourite jeans deserve a second life, and so does the planet.

reading.title: Made to Measure
text: The waiter at the corner café remembered the old man. "He spoke Portuguese like the old Cape Verdean grandfathers, soft, like a song. He asked me where he could still eat a proper cachupa. I sent him to Dona Celeste."

Dona Celeste ran a small Cape Verdean restaurant three streets away. She was seventy-five and had known Zé in the seventies. "He had golden hands. And honest, honest like bread. If you dropped a coin, Zé would run after you down the street to give it back. When they said he had stolen from the Fonsecas, nobody here believed it. But who listens to us?"

"Then why did he run away?" Rafiq asked. Dona Celeste explained that in the summer of 1975, when Cape Verde became independent, a new law meant that many people born in the colonies, like Zé, were suddenly no longer Portuguese. "Now imagine a foreigner with a police report saying he stole money from a white man's safe. With a witness. Zé didn't run because he was guilty. He ran because he knew exactly what would happen to him if he stayed." He crossed into Spain and France on foot, and finally reached England.

In January, Zé had stayed with her cousin for ten days, asking whether Lurdes was well and happy. Now he had gone back to England for a heart operation. "He wanted to see this street once more, just in case. He was wearing a camel coat. He'd had it made forty years ago, by himself, and had never once had it altered."

Meanwhile, the repair café had become famous. Bia filmed Lurdes's hands turning a torn sleeve into something better than new and posted the video with the caption: "My best friend's grandmother is 68 and she can fix anything. Except the housing market." In a few days it had been watched more than four hundred thousand times. Rafiq had to set up a booking website in one night. "This is what progress is supposed to look like," he said. "Technology that helps an old woman keep her shop open."

Not everyone was happy. Bia's father, who worked for Tagus Living, told her she would regret posting the video. "I told him I didn't regret posting it at all," Bia said. "I only regretted not posting it sooner."

Then Mr Okafor brought his grey jacket to be repaired. Lurdes examined the buttonholes and went very still. "He learned in Lisbon, your tailor. I only ever knew one person who finished a buttonhole like this." Mr Okafor laughed and took the jacket back. That evening, Rafiq came down from the roof. "My father has made up his mind. In July, we're moving to London. All of us. Me too."

writing.model: I think social media can help local communities, but only if people use it for more than likes. A good example is the video of a grandmother repairing clothes in Lisbon. It went viral, and suddenly hundreds of people wanted to have their clothes fixed instead of buying new ones. A small shop that nobody noticed became the centre of the neighbourhood. That is real progress: technology helping people stay where they are. In my town, we got the council to repair a dangerous playground after parents posted photos of it on a Facebook group. Without the pressure online, I'm sure it would still be broken. However, social media also has a dark side. The same video that helps a shop can make a street so popular with tourists that rents go up and residents have to leave. So my answer is yes, but carefully. Social media is a tool, and like scissors, it depends on whose hands are holding it.

reading.title: Smoke
text: March was the month when everything began to fall apart, slowly at first and then all at once. First, the water was cut off for three days "for urgent maintenance". Then two electricians in Tagus Living overalls turned up with a letter from Rui. "We're getting the wiring checked before the sale," they said, and left behind a fuse box with a new grey cover and a smell of hot plastic. Then the Nepalese cooks found an unsigned note under their door: "Foreigners with no contract should think about their future."

"It's a campaign," said Rafiq. It was the first thing he had said to Marta in nine days, since she had answered his news about London with a cold "Good luck". "They're trying to wear us down. Water, noise, threats. People give up and take the money just to make it stop." Marta apologised, and he smiled for the first time in nine days.

At school, the 11.º classes held a debate: "Progress: who pays the bill?" Rafiq argued that progress was always paid for by somebody who wasn't in the room. Marta argued that a city where the people who cook the food and clean the offices can't afford to live is not progress: it is a postcard.

Then Bia found an email on her father's laptop. It was from Ricardo Vidal: "Rua dos Cavaleiros: pressure measures in progress as agreed. The old lady and the Bangladeshis should come round by April. Shop wiring taken care of." Bia did not shout. She put the laptop in front of her father and asked one question: "Did you agree to this?" He read it twice, locked himself in his study for three hours, and came out on the phone to a lawyer. "He didn't know," Bia said. "He said, 'I've never once been to that street.' Maybe that's the whole problem."

But finding something out is not the same as stopping it. At the end of March, Rui signed the promissory contract. "I've got debts, Tia. I can't afford to be sentimental." That night, Marta finally told Lurdes about Zé's visit and his heart operation. "I'll never forget seeing him at that table," Lurdes said. "Thank you for telling me, filha. Next time, don't wait a month."

On the last Saturday of the term, the repair café had its biggest day ever. Marta fell asleep over her Physics book and woke at ten to three with a strange taste in her mouth. Smoke. Her grandmother's bed was empty, and so was the nail by the door. Below, a thin grey ribbon of smoke was curling out from under the door of the shop.

reading.title: The Letter in the Tin
text: Never in her life had Marta moved so fast. With Rafiq and Bishal, she ran into the smoke and found Lurdes on the floor beside the cutting table, coughing, holding the biscuit tin against her chest. No sooner had they reached the street than the shop window cracked with a sound like a gunshot. Lurdes spent five days in hospital with smoke in her lungs and a broken wrist. The shop survived, in a way. The back wall was black, but the old oak table was only scorched.

The fire had started in the fuse box. "Someone did work on this installation recently," the fire officer told Marta, "and it can't have been a qualified electrician. Whoever did it must have known it was dangerous." Not only did Henrique Lemos give the police Vidal's emails, but he also resigned from Tagus Living. By the middle of April, the company announced that it was withdrawing from the project. "So we won," said Bia. "Rui still has debts," said Rafiq. "He'll find another buyer."

The 3.º período brought the work experience week in Leicester that Mr Okafor had organised. Marta did not want to leave her grandmother, but Lurdes insisted. First there were CVs to write in English. "Under no circumstances," said Mr Okafor, "should you write that you are 'a hard worker and a team player'. Everybody writes that. Tell me something only you could say."

Marta's mother, Sofia, came home from Luxembourg to look after Lurdes. Marta practised her arguments for a class debate on her: "Should young Portuguese people go abroad to work?" "On the one hand, you earn more and learn a lot. On the other hand, you leave everything behind. Moreover, the country trains nurses and engineers and then loses them." "It isn't a debate when it's your own life," Sofia said. "Although I don't regret going, I regret what it cost. Mainly you. Should the hospital here offer me a decent contract, I'd come back tomorrow."

The night before the trip, Lurdes gave Marta the envelope she had written in 1975 to José Varela, the one that had never been posted. "I know you'll look for him. If you find him, give him this. I'd rather he heard it from me than from anyone else. It's not for you to open, filha." This time, Marta promised.

In the morning, she went to say goodbye and stopped at the door. Mr Okafor was sitting by the bed, speaking soft, musical Portuguese: "He's recovering well. The operation went well. He asked me to tell you..." Marta pushed the door open. "Since when," she said, "do you speak Portuguese?"

In my opinion, going abroad can be a good decision, but it should be a choice, not an obligation. On the one hand, working in another country has clear advantages. Salaries are often higher, and young professionals gain experience, learn languages and become more independent. Moreover, many of them come back with new ideas that help Portugal. On the other hand, emigration has a cost. Families are separated, and grandparents see their grandchildren only on a screen. Furthermore, the country pays to educate doctors, nurses and engineers, and then other countries benefit from their work. Therefore, I believe the real problem is not that young people leave, but that many of them feel they have no alternative. Although travelling and working abroad can be enriching, nobody should have to emigrate just to pay the rent. To sum up, Portugal should create the conditions for young people to stay, so that leaving is an adventure and not an escape.

reading.title: A City with No Majority
text: Mr Okafor's mother was from Cape Verde, so he had spoken Portuguese since he was born. "I asked him not to tell you," Lurdes said. "Don't be angry with him. Be angry with me." But there was no time for anger. The taxi was waiting, and Mr Okafor promised to explain everything in Leicester.

"In this city, there is no majority," Mr Okafor told the students as they walked down Belgrave Road, past sari shops, sweet shops and jewellers' windows full of gold. "Every group is a minority. Nobody is the main character." "Does it work?" asked Bia. "Most days. Not every day. People need work, and homes, and to feel that nobody is looking down on them. Where they have that, it works quite well."

Rafiq was placed at an engineering firm that designed footbridges, Bia at a law firm that defended tenants, and Marta at Second Stitch, a small workshop that repaired clothes and taught sewing to refugees. "You must wear these gloves for the steam press," said Agnieszka, the owner. "You needn't bring lunch; we all eat together. And you should ask if you don't understand something." From Agnieszka, Marta learnt that Joe Varela had been the best tailor in the city. He had started in a hosiery factory, working night shifts, and later opened his own shop near the Clock Tower. After a heart operation, he was still in hospital.

In a café, Mr Okafor finally told her the truth. Joe had helped his mother when she arrived in Leicester, alone, at nineteen, and later became Daniel's godfather. Last summer, Joe had received a letter from a dying man in Portugal, António Fonseca, and had asked Daniel to find out whether Lurdes was well. "I asked to teach in Lisbon, at the school nearest Rua dos Cavaleiros. Then I read the class list, and there you were." "Should I have told you? Probably. But it wasn't my secret."

Mr Okafor said that Joe did not want anyone from Lisbon to see him so ill. Marta waited one day. Then she lied to Agnieszka about a dentist's appointment and took a bus to the hospital. Not until she was standing at the entrance did she realise that she had no plan at all.

In bed six, by the window, lay a thin old man with long, clean tailor's hands. Marta sat beside him for a long time. When he opened his eyes, his whole face changed. "Lurdes?" he whispered. "No. I'm her granddaughter. I'm Marta." He looked at her chin, her eyes, her dark curly hair. Then he took her hand. "Then you are mine too," said Zé Varela.

reading.title: Fonseca & Varela
text: Zé asked Marta to read Lurdes's letter aloud, because his eyes were too weak. "Zé," she read, "they say you took the money. I don't believe it, not for one minute. I have to tell you something, and I wish I could say it to your face. I am going to have a baby. Our baby. The doctor thinks it will be born in February. Tell me where you are and I will come. Your Lurdes. Lisbon, 10 July 1975."

February. Her mother's birthday was the fourteenth of February. Only then did Marta understand what she had carried across Europe in her backpack. Her mother was Zé's daughter, and Zé was her grandfather.

Zé had known since the summer before. Tó had written to him before he died. In 1975, Tó had gambling debts. He took the money from the safe himself and, when the police came, he needed a thief. "I was the easiest thief in Lisbon," said Zé. Tó told Fernando he had seen Zé with the box, and Fernando, young and in love with Lurdes, believed him and signed. Tó never posted Lurdes's letter, and he hid all of Zé's letters under the cutting table. "Fernando knew the baby was yours," Tó had written, "and raised her as his own. I took fifty years from you both."

The flowers, Zé explained, arrived every year on the last day of September because that was the day in 1973 when he had first walked into the shop asking for work. "Every year I thought, this year she will write back. She never did." "She didn't know," said Marta. "Had I known then," he said, "nothing in this world would have kept me away."

Not all endings are neat. Vidal was charged, although the case would take years. Rui, after reading his father's confession, sold the building to the city council, which rented old buildings at fair prices, for much less than Tagus had offered. The Ahmeds would move to London in July, but Rafiq would stay to finish school. Sofia signed a contract with a Lisbon hospital.

On the night of Santo António, a taxi stopped at the bottom of Rua dos Cavaleiros. Zé got out, with a walking stick and a camel coat far too hot for June. Above the shop window, a new sign said: FONSECA & VARELA. REPAIRS, ALTERATIONS, SECOND LIVES. "That coat is too hot for June," said Lurdes. "I know," said Zé. "It's the only one good enough." Then he turned to Sofia. "You have her chin." Later, through the window, Marta watched an old woman measuring an old man for a summer jacket and telling him, as she had in 1973, that he was holding his scissors wrong.

writing.model: Most families have secrets, and many people believe that keeping them is a way of protecting the people we love. In my view, a secret can be justified for a short time, but it almost always causes more damage than the truth. It is true that there are moments when silence seems kind. For example, parents may not tell a young child about a serious illness until the child is old enough to understand. Furthermore, some secrets belong to another person, and it is not our right to reveal them. Nevertheless, long secrets tend to grow. In The Cutting Table, Tó hid a few letters to protect himself, and as a result two people lost fifty years and a daughter grew up without knowing her own father. Moreover, the people who keep secrets also suffer: Lurdes carried hers for half a century. To sum up, I believe that we should tell difficult truths carefully and at the right moment, but we should tell them. A secret may protect people today, but it usually hurts them tomorrow.

sebenta.title: Tenses: present and past
sebenta.html:
Present Simple

FormUseExamples
I/you/we/they work
he/she/it works
neg.: don't / doesn't + verb
quest.: Do / Does + subject + verb?		 • habits and routines
• permanent situations, facts
• timetables and schedules
• with adverbs of frequency		 She works in a bank.
Water boils at 100 °C.
The train leaves at 9.15.
I always get up early.

Adverbs of frequency: always · usually · often · sometimes · rarely / seldom · hardly ever · never. They go before the main verb but after be: He never complains. / He is never late.

Present Continuous

FormUseExamples
am / is / are + verb-ing • actions happening now
• temporary situations
• changing situations
• fixed future arrangements
• annoying habits (+ always)		 She's talking on the phone.
I'm staying with a friend this week.
Prices are rising.
We're meeting at 8 tomorrow.
He's always losing his keys!
Stative verbs are not normally used in continuous tenses: know, believe, understand, want, need, like, love, hate, prefer, belong, own, seem, mean. I want a coffee (not I'm wanting). Some change meaning: I think it's good (opinion) / I'm thinking about it (process).

Past Simple

FormUseExamples
regular: verb + -ed
irregular: 2nd column (p. 14)
neg.: didn't + verb
quest.: Did + subject + verb?		 • finished actions at a definite time in the past
• a sequence of past events
• past habits and states		 We visited Rome last year.
She opened the door and went in.
I lived in Porto as a child.

Time markers: yesterday · last week/year · two days ago · in 2015 · when I was a child.

Past Continuous

FormUseExamples
was / were + verb-ing • action in progress at a past moment
• background to a shorter action (past simple)
• two parallel actions		 At 8 pm I was having dinner.
I was walking home when it started to rain.
While I was cooking, he was reading.
Past Simple vs Past Continuous: when + past simple interrupts; while / as + past continuous gives the background. The phone rang while I was sleeping.

sebenta.title: Tenses: perfect tenses
sebenta.html:
Present Perfect Simple

FormUseExamples
have / has + past participle (3rd column, p. 14) • unfinished past (started in the past, continues now) → for / since
• life experience → ever, never, before
• recent news / results evident now → just, already, yet
• tasks done / not done up to now		 I've lived here for ten years / since 2016.
Have you ever been to London?
She has just arrived. · I've lost my keys!
I've already finished; he hasn't started yet.

Markers: for · since · ever · never · just · already · yet · so far · recently · lately · this week · today · how long…?

Present Perfect Continuous

FormUseExamples
have / has been + verb-ing • unfinished activity, emphasis on duration
• repeated actions up to now
• activity just stopped, results evident now		 I've been studying for three hours.
She's been calling you all morning.
You're red – have you been running?
Simple vs Continuous: simple = result / how many (I've written three emails); continuous = activity / how long (I've been writing emails all day). Stative verbs → simple only (I've known him for years).
Past Simple vs Present Perfect: finished time (yesterday, in 2010, ago) → past simple; time up to now (today, this year, ever, since) → present perfect. I saw him yesterday. / I have seen him today. Note: been = went and came back; gone = not back yet.

Past Perfect Simple

FormUseExamples
had + past participle • an action completed before another past action or moment ("the past of the past")
• with by the time, after, before, when, already, never…before
• in reported speech and 3rd conditional		 When I arrived, the film had already started.
She had never flown before that day.
By 2020 they had moved twice.

Past Perfect Continuous

FormUseExamples
had been + verb-ing • activity in progress up to a past moment, emphasis on duration
• cause of a past situation		 He had been waiting for an hour when the bus came.
Her eyes were red – she had been crying.

Tenses together: I have known Ana since we were at school. · It has been raining since I got up.

sebenta.title: The passive voice
sebenta.html:
Form: be (in the right tense) + past participle. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject. The agent is introduced by by, and is omitted when unknown, obvious or unimportant. We use the passive to focus on the action or the result, in formal, scientific and news writing.

TenseActivePassive
Present SimpleThey clean the rooms daily.The rooms are cleaned daily.
Present ContinuousThey are cleaning the rooms.The rooms are being cleaned.
Past SimpleThey cleaned the rooms.The rooms were cleaned.
Past ContinuousThey were cleaning the rooms.The rooms were being cleaned.
Present PerfectThey have cleaned the rooms.The rooms have been cleaned.
Past PerfectThey had cleaned the rooms.The rooms had been cleaned.
Future (will)They will clean the rooms.The rooms will be cleaned.
Going toThey are going to clean the rooms.The rooms are going to be cleaned.
Modal verbsThey must / should clean the rooms.The rooms must / should be cleaned.
Modal perfectThey should have cleaned the rooms.The rooms should have been cleaned.
Infinitive / -ingI want them to clean it. · I hate people watching me.I want it to be cleaned. · I hate being watched.
  • Two objects (give, send, offer, show, tell, pay…): two passives are possible; the person is usually the subject. They gave me a prize. → I was given a prize. / A prize was given to me.
  • Questions: Was the letter sent? · When was it built? Negative: It wasn't delivered.
  • Verbs with prepositions keep them: The children were looked after by their aunt.
  • Get + past participle is informal: He got fired. · My bike got stolen.

Impersonal passive (reporting verbs)

With say, think, believe, know, report, expect, consider, claim, suppose, used to report opinions or facts without naming the source:

StructureExamples
It is / was + past participle + that + clauseIt is said that he is very rich. · It was believed that the Earth was flat.
Subject + is / are + past participle + to + infinitive (same time)He is said to be very rich. · They are expected to arrive soon.
Subject + is / are + past participle + to have + past participle (earlier time)He is believed to have left the country. · The Earth was thought to be flat.

Causative: have / get something done

have / get + object + past participle = someone else does the action for us (a service). I had my hair cut yesterday. · We're getting the car repaired. · She has had her phone fixed. Compare: I cut my hair (I did it myself). Also for unpleasant events: He had his wallet stolen. Have / get someone do / to do something = make or persuade: I'll have my assistant call you. · I got him to help me.

Defining relative clauses

Give essential information to identify the noun. No commas. That can replace who / which. The pronoun can be omitted when it is the object of the clause: The film (which) we saw was great. · The woman (who) you met is my aunt. But not when it is the subject: The woman who called is my aunt.

Add extra information about a noun already identified; between commas. That is not used and the pronoun cannot be omitted. My brother, who lives in Faro, is a doctor. · Sintra, which is near Lisbon, is beautiful. Which can refer to the whole previous clause: He arrived late, which annoyed everyone.

Prepositions usually go at the end: the house (which) I grew up in; formal: the house in which I grew up.
